Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: FIRM: Fisher-Informed Retention Merging for Federated LLM Unlearning
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Federated LLM unlearning addresses targeted knowledge removal when forget and retain data remain distributed across private clients and are inaccessible to the server. The resulting locally trained adapters encode conflicting objectives, making their aggregation fundamentally different from conventional federated optimization. A key failure mode is magnitude explosion, whereby unnormalized cross-client aggregation increases the merged update magnitude and degrades retained utility under stronger unlearning. We propose FIRM (Fisher-Informed Retention Merging), a single-round framework for stable and retention-aware server-side aggregation. FIRM uses client-local Fisher statistics as a unified sensitivity signal to construct a Fisher-normalized base merge and impose explicit control over retain-sensitive parameters. Its second-order retention projection admits a unique minimum-distance solution, while the corresponding dual scales with the number of retain clients rather than the model dimension. Experiments across WMDP, TOFU, and MUSE-HP using Zephyr-7B and Llama-3-8B show utility gains at comparable forgetting on WMDP and MUSE-HP, with metric-dependent trade-offs on TOFU. Controlled comparisons support benefits of the combined base merge and additional retention correction at selected operating points.

Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.title: Encoded but Exposed: Language Embeddings can Reveal More Than They Should in Recommender Systems
Artificial Intelligence (Agents & Multi-.summary: Language embeddings are increasingly used in recommenders to represent item content, but their privacy risks remain poorly understood. We study whether item embeddings can reveal item identities when an adversary has access to auxiliary item text from external sources. We show that a simple cosine-similarity attack can recover item identities with high mean reciprocal rank across language models and candidate-set settings on two real-world datasets. Leakage is strongest when the adversary's partial information overlaps with the victim representation, but it also persists through semantic alignment between independently sourced descriptions. We further show that item leakage can propagate to user re-identification from sparse ratings. Finally, we evaluate obfuscated descriptions as a mitigation and find a clear leakage-utility tradeoff.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: A Gradual Probabilistic Lambda Calculus
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
Probabilistic programming languages extend ordinary programming languages with the ability to sample values from probability distributions. Type systems can establish invariants of such programs, for instance by assigning to a program a distribution over types that specifies the probability of each kind of outcome. However, adopting such a type discipline can be cumbersome or overly conservative.
  Gradual typing addresses this problem by supporting a smooth transition between static and dynamic checking, and has been successfully applied for languages with different constructs and type abstractions. Nevertheless, its benefits have never been explored in the context of probabilistic languages.
  In this work, we present and formalize GLANG, a gradual source probabilistic lambda calculus. GLANG includes a binary probabilistic choice operator and allows programmers to gradually introduce/remove static type---and probability---annotations. The static semantics of GLANG heavily relies on the notion of probabilistic couplings, as required for defining several relations, such as consistency, precision, and consistent transitivity. The dynamic semantics of GLANG is given via elaboration to the target language TLANG, which features a distribution-based semantics interpreting programs as probability distributions over final values. Regarding the language metatheory, we establish that TLANG---and therefore also GLANG---is type safe and satisfies two of the so-called refined criteria for gradual languages, namely, that it is a conservative extension of a fully static variant and that it satisfies (a restricted form of) the gradual guarantee, behaving smoothly with respect to type precision. The metatheory is mechanized in the Lean 4 proof assistant.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Are We Testing the Wrong Quantum Bugs? A Study of Fault Representation Gaps in Quantum Software Testing
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Quantum software relies on compilers, intermediate representations, and execution frameworks that transform programs before execution. Faults in these components can change the behavior of otherwise correct quantum programs. Yet quantum testing techniques are often evaluated using mutation-generated faults and curated bug benchmarks. We investigate how well the faults represented by these artifacts reflect those encountered in modern quantum software. We audit four quantum mutation-testing tools and three curated bug benchmarks, and collect 410 verified bugs from ten quantum software repositories over two years. We classify faults from all three sources into a common taxonomy of 56 bug families and compare their representation across mutation operators, curated benchmarks, and recent real-world bugs. The mutation tools support 20 bug families, and curated benchmarks add 15 more. Yet only 56 of the 410 real-world bugs (13.7%) belong to families represented by either source; the remaining 354 (86.3%) belong to families absent from both. The largest unrepresented families concern compiler transformations (66 bugs), type handling (53), and input validation (47). Unlike local gate or statement changes, these faults often depend on intermediate representations, compiler pipelines, input types, or dependency versions. Existing mutation operators primarily modify circuits and program constructs, whereas many real-world faults arise in the compilers, representations, and framework interfaces that process them. Addressing this gap requires looking beyond circuit-level faults toward testing semantic preservation across compiler transformations, correctness at representation boundaries, and interactions between software components. Our study provides empirical evidence to guide fault models and benchmarks that capture these mechanisms and preserve the contexts needed to reproduce them.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: FAOPs: Normal Forms and an Algebra for AI Agent Workflows
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Organizations increasingly encode operational procedures as multi-step agent skills, here called Agent Operating Procedures (AOPs), that must be traceable, auditable, reproducible, access-controlled, and bounded in time and cost, requirements that regulated sectors make mandatory. Yet AOPs are typically kept as coarse-grained files, in which steps bundle actions, copied procedures drift apart, any step may reach any tool, and refactoring goes unchecked. We present Functional Agent Operating Procedures (FAOP), a formal theory that brings database-grade discipline to AI agent workflows. FAOP recasts each workflow as a typed function over scoped state and subjects an entire library to four progressive normal forms: Decomposed (FNF-1) splits a workflow into atomic steps, Typed (FNF-2) makes its data flow explicit and type-checked, Factored (FNF-3) gives each shared procedure a single canonical definition so a change propagates instead of drifting, and Scoped (FNF-4) confines every step to least-privilege tool access. Once normalized, every atomic step is a separate entity with a declared contract and can be type-checked, scope-confined, bounded, tested, traced, and audited on its own. A FAOP algebra of provably sound equalities turns refactoring and parallelization into compiler rewrites; orthogonal extensions add verified termination (+V), optimization (+O), and time and cost bounds (+B); and an architectural-level classifier (0-3) determines whether a workflow needs AI at all. Together, these make integrity, isolation, typing, termination, cost, and optimization compile-time concerns across the whole library, not runtime hopes. We implement the theory in SkillBase, an AOP management system (what PostgreSQL is to data, SkillBase is to AOPs), together with a separate executor that enforces these guarantees at run time. A worked financial workflow illustrates the approach end to end.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 28 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Bidirectional Elaborators à la Carte
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
Surface syntax in proof assistants like Rocq, Lean, Agda, and Idris is highly implicit, lacking many details that are needed for user-written code to denote precisely defined mathematical objects. Elaboration is an algorithm that accounts for these details by translating surface syntax to an explicit enough core syntax. The reliability and predictability of elaboration relies on several critical properties of the core type system, including decidability of judgemental equality and the injectivity of type constructors; these dependencies are witnessed in a concrete system by explicit calls to conversion checking and weak-head reduction subroutines.
  We introduce a dependently typed monadic domain specific language for the executable specification of correct-by-construction elaboration algorithms that is abstracted from any particular representation of normal forms or algorithm for conversion checking. In particular, we represent a bidirectionally typed surface language for Martin-Löf type theory by shallow embedding in this DSL so that the translation of surface terms into core terms amounts to elementary equational calculation. This translation is correct by construction in the sense that it cannot produce ill-typed terms, and is automatically stable under judgemental equality of core terms and even under substitution; from the latter property, we obtain a new denotational interpretation of the suspension of elaboration problems. Finally, a concrete elaboration algorithm is extracted by algebraic means from a presheaf model of the DSL built out of the bi-initial natural model of Martin-Löf type theory.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: Add further discussion of related work; other minor wording and typographical improvements

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Enhancing Knowledge Density via Hierarchical Context Pruning for Retrieval-Augmented Repository-Level Code Completion
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has advanced repository-level code completion by retrieving external code snippets, API documentation, or type definitions to expand the model's contextual awareness. However, under the finite token budget of the context window, existing retrieval-augmented methods often saturate the budget with highly similar or even redundant code, which not only wastes tokens but also suppresses critical cross-file dependencies, preventing synergistic interaction between semantically similar reference snippets and cross-file dependency definitions. Therefore, further gains are limited by low knowledge density in the retrieved context rather than by model capacity. We propose SaraCoder, a retrieval-augmented framework that enhances knowledge density via hierarchical context pruning under a fixed context budget. A Hierarchical Feature Optimization module prunes an over-complete candidate pool in four stages. The freed tokens are then allocated to an External-Aware Identifier Disambiguator, which selectively injects only the most necessary cross-file dependency definitions. SaraCoder transforms context construction into a budget-aware optimization problem, balancing reference snippets and cross-file dependencies to build a context that is both knowledge-dense and semantically complete. Experiments on CrossCodeEval and RepoEval-Updated, across multiple backbone code LLMs, show that SaraCoder consistently outperforms strong RAG baselines such as GraphCoder and Repocoder in both code-level and identifier-level metrics, without increasing token usage, and yields synergistic gains when combined with other cross-file methods.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Coexponential Exploration in the Clef Programming Language
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Clef was created as a concurrent programming language whose compiler tracks state ownership, waiting computations and request dependencies. We develop a coexponential account of stateful services and their client pools within this design. Delimited continuations retain the computation and resources needed to complete each interaction. These structures give our compiler premises for verifying service composition and preserving it through native lowering to multiple hardware targets. We connect finite actor state transitions to the initial, service and final rules of a coexponential server. A separate operational account relates actor dispatch to single-use continuation frames. We prove state-ownership and reply preservation, give a finite communication-summary analysis, and derive circular-wait exclusion under stated assumptions. A further result identifies when changing service order preserves both state and replies. Our Program Semantic Graph retains these facts through compilation. We are researching reusable proofs to confirm the ownership and communication interfaces, while our BAREWire implementation connects message meaning to its unboxed representation across respective endpoints. A distributed worker example preserves request identity across suspension, reordered replies and boundary conversion. Urschel's growth bounds inform a solver service; a distributed ADM update additionally preserves joint samples, metric evidence and request identity. Our two-category account connects component refinement, reusable proof terms and native realization. Protocols determine the admissible interactions, continuations expose their storage requirements, and retained dependencies support differential compilation. Developers can express ordinary stateful services while the compiler carries the conditions for their correct composition across execution targets.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 36 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Updated for contributions from Karwowski et al. and clarified Padovani's fair-termination result

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Negative and Fractional Types in the Fidelity Framework
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Programs routinely create temporary data, retain state and revisit earlier results. Negative and fractional types benefit those activities in a type-resolved account of computation. Negative values redirect evaluation. Fractional values introduce value-specific auxiliary data and discharge it after a computation restores the required value. We develop both as first-class computational forms in our Clef design, using Chen and Sabry's directed, value-indexed calculus and distinguishing James and Sabry's logic-variable search interpretation. Our Program Semantic Graph retains their value identities and resource uses, enabling Composer to preserve their behavior through MLIR operations and native realization. In this paper, a negative-type counter and a fractional workspace calculation demonstrate the two constructions. Local proofs establish preservation of matching and independent resource discharge. Dimensional inference and proof terms supply premises through our four verification tiers. The applications connect deferred reverse computation to gradient calculations without an activation tape, and checked inverse steps to in-memory event recovery. A finite reconstruction horizon governs the exchange between storage and recomputation. We derive its error recurrence and show where Urschel's elimination-growth bounds can support a realized inverse step. Bayesian updates and quantum circuits supply further computational cases, including temporary workspace, measurement and a worked adiabatic schedule. Exact matching, bounded reconstruction and physical realization retain their respective contracts. The resulting architecture makes the information needed to run, reverse or complete a computation available to the compiler. Libraries can expose these operations through familiar interfaces while their retained structure supports unboxed execution and differential compilation across targets.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 27 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Updated for contributions from Karwowski et al

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Fixed-Point Scaffolding in the Clef Programming Language
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Native compilation changes how a program represents values and performs operations from processor to processor. In our view, proofs that justify source-level decisions must remain connected to those changes. We develop fixed-point scaffolding for this continuity in Clef and our Composer compiler. Our Program Semantic Graph retains types, joint constraints and proof dependencies. A thin MLIR middle end witnesses their settled consequences for native CPU, GPU, NPU and FPGA realization. The account connects nanopass traversal with preservation contracts, structural theorems and adjoint interfaces between reasoning modes. Four verification tiers organize automatic inference and reusable domain and system proofs, with probabilistic relations admitted at Tier 4. Established lower-tier facts can directly support richer derivations. We state conditions for composing lowering contracts and assembling compatible program segments, then show how their dependencies govern differential compilation after an edit. A worked foreign-call boundary follows source ranges through argument marshaling, the actual call and return conversion. Current FFI mechanisms bind checking evidence to those witnessed operations. A recent paper from Urschel provides elimination-growth bounds that supply a quantitative example. Reusable premises inform representation and error contracts that retain their sampling, arithmetic and exceptional-path assumptions. A further example admits value-indexed pairing through ordinary MLIR operations, connecting this scaffold to negative and fractional types. Together these constructions explain how a thin middle end can carry the consequences of rich source proofs into unboxed computation graphs. Integrity and efficiency share the same retained evidence. It justifies native realizations and identifies which analyses, proofs and lowered fragments remain reusable during development.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 25 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Updated for contributions from Karwowski et al

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Decidable By Construction: Design-Time Verification for Truly Fearless Systems
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Concurrency, parallelism and distributed execution become truly fearless when the compiler tracks wait-for edges, proves multi-threaded work is sound and preserves distributed boundary contracts. In this design, our Composer compiler preserves proofs while lowering Clef directly to native CPU, GPU, NPU and FPGA code, without translation through C or vendor APIs. Our Program Semantic Graph retains the values, relationships and premises that justify BAREWire's unboxed boundary contracts. And C & C++ interfacing is an explicit marshaling boundary, with proofs tied to actual arguments, conversions and returned values. Four verification tiers connect an account of our design. Tier 1 supplies structural inference, founded on principal dimensional types. Tier 2 generates and checks local arithmetic, representation, and computational integrity at the node level. Tier 3 instantiates reusable domain and system lemmas, including distributed proofs supported by Iris, Actris and Aneris. Tiers 1-3 require no developer annotations, with a quotation based lemma library design to extend coverage as use cases expand. Tier 4 admits computational and probabilistic relational proofs, with project annotations identifying the required relations. We extend the same library direction toward recognizing relational constructions from hypergraph structure. A formal composition rule connects arithmetic, ownership, protocol and realization evidence. Our worked distributed reduction preserves one specified result across concurrent workers, reordered arrivals and boundary mappings. Its probabilistic extension carries worker and conversion error with an explicit failure budget. With recent work by Urschel, we show bounds supply a relevant source of reusable proof terms. These constructions make verification a core engineering discipline for truly fearless programs and systems across a variety of hardware targets.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 34 pages, 0 figures, 4 tables. Updated for contributions from Karwowski et al

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Dimensional Type Systems and Deterministic Memory Management
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: We present a dimensional type system whose annotations remain available through the stages that require them, allowing numeric representation and deterministic memory management to be resolved within a single Program Semantic Graph (PSG). Based on Andrew Kennedy's Units of Measure, dimensions constrain admissible operations and the application of domain laws, forming our Native Type Universe (NTU). Range analysis combines those constraints with values, guards, and declared boundaries. A covering representation then determines word width and memory footprint, which participate in allocation and transfer decisions alongside lifetime and target constraints. Our Dimensional Type System (DTS) extends Hindley-Milner inference with abelian-group unification. Within that algebraic fragment, inference is decidable and admits principal types. Measures form part of source-level type identity, while numeric width and storage layout are coeffects resolved from context. A known range that exceeds every available representation produces an error at representation commitment. During program elaboration, unresolved facts can remain pending while further context is supplied. Deterministic Memory Management (DMM) uses the same graph to relate escape paths to storage lifetimes. Closure capture, return, and by-reference use supply different lifetime requirements. Allocation follows the lifetime classification and the platform's declared storage capabilities. Our unique implementation of a posit quire illustrates the interaction: exact accumulation requires a suitable numeric format, adequate capacity, and storage that persists across the accumulation. We also examine how these constraints would apply to automatic differentiation. A shared graph would allow language services to present dimensional resolution and proof status alongside the reasons for representation and placement decisions.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 26 pages, 0 figures, 7 tables. Updated for contributions from Karwowski et al

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: The Program Hypergraph: Multi-Way Relational Structure for Geometric Algebra, Spatial Compute, and Physics-Aware Compilation
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Source code organizes a program as expressions and declarations, which a compiler can represent as an abstract syntax tree (AST). Some compilers introduce a further abstraction of the computation as a graph. Nodes represent operations, while connections record how values pass between them and how execution proceeds. Yet these connections can leave the full scope of conditions governing a computation implicit. Developers may then need defensive checks, rely on compiler hacks, pragmas, and implementation-specific code to maintain those conditions as the program evolves. Our thesis is that a hypergraph more faithfully represents complex computation across all targets by making joint constraints inherent to its structure, with an overall less burdensome design-time API. Our Program Hypergraph (PHG) extends our Semantic Graph with relations that connect across an operation's participants, their dependencies, and the invariants they must preserve. Joint resolution in the graph guides lowering into standard Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR). Satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) checks intrinsic to the graph discharge applicable proof obligations. Supporting information remains available until the decisions that require it are complete. As a primary benefit, verification follows from the rules used to construct and transform the graph. For properties established this way before execution, the generated program needs no added runtime checks, no 'boxing' or 'tagging' or other managed runtime support. We develop this account through geometric algebra, shared-memory capacity, and spatial placement, distinguishing structural guarantees from numerical and resource obligations that require further evidence. The proposed integration makes the same information available at design-time, so engineers can inspect the consequences of a choice before it becomes an implementation constraint.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 27 pages, 0 figures, 4 tables. Updated for contributions from Karwowski et al

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Volition Elicitation: Operational Semantics for People and Their Machines
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
The most prevalent distributed systems today include people and their personal machines (smartphones), and computations in them are driven by people's volitions. Volition-guarded multiagent atomic transactions were proposed as an abstract specification language for such systems, in which a transaction has a precondition on the machine states of its participants and is guarded by the volitions of some of them.
  Here we develop an abstraction cascade that derives smartphone apps from such specifications and prove it correct down to the base programming language, GLP. The cascade consists of: (1) communicating volitional agents (CVA), which implement every local volition-guarded specification with simple guards, correctly, and completely for its strongly fair runs, by two-phase commit coordinated by the initiating agent; (2) volition-guarded GLP (vGLP), an extension of GLP with volitional procedures, whose goals put an interactively-typed question to the person, into which that implementation compiles; and (3) GLP, which implements vGLP by eliciting the person's answers through the widgets of their interactive types, correctly, and completely for complete widgets. We demonstrate the approach on three grassroots platforms --- a social graph, a social network, and currencies: a compiler carries the social graph and the currencies down the cascade to GLP programs that run with scripted persons, and earlier programs of the three run as mini-apps of one smartphone app.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: SEVerA: Verified Synthesis of Self-Evolving Agents
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Recent advances have shown the effectiveness of self-evolving LLM agents on tasks such as program repair and scientific discovery. In this paradigm, a planner LLM synthesizes an agent program that invokes parametric models, including LLMs, which are then tuned per task to improve performance. However, existing self-evolving agent frameworks provide no formal guarantees of safety or correctness. Because such programs are often executed autonomously on unseen inputs, this lack of guarantees raises reliability and security concerns. We formulate agentic code generation as a constrained learning problem, combining hard formal specifications with soft objectives capturing task utility. We introduce Formally Guarded Generative Models (FGGM), which allow the planner LLM to specify a formal output contract for each generative model call using first-order logic. Each FGGM call wraps the underlying model in a rejection sampler with a verified fallback, ensuring every returned output satisfies the contract for any input and parameter setting. Building on FGGM, we present SEVerA (Self-Evolving Verified Agents), a three-stage framework: Search synthesizes candidate parametric programs containing FGGM calls; Verification proves correctness with respect to hard constraints for all parameter values, reducing the problem to unconstrained learning; and Learning applies scalable gradient-based optimization, including GRPO-style fine-tuning, to improve the soft objective while preserving correctness. We evaluate SEVerA on Dafny program verification, symbolic math synthesis, and policy-compliant agentic tool use ($τ^2$-bench). Across tasks, SEVerA achieves zero constraint violations while improving performance over unconstrained and SOTA baselines, showing that formal behavioral constraints not only guarantee correctness but also steer synthesis toward higher-quality agents.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: First Formally Verified Self-Evolving LLM Agents

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Normalization by Evaluation with Substitutions as Operations
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: In previous works on normalization by evaluation (NbE) with an untyped domain model, explicit substitutions are a major decision choice, which, in retrospect, is taken to simplify subsequent semantic proofs. This choice hence is taken for a purely technical reason. In addition, there is no obvious lemma to test the completeness of the definition or the laws for explicit substitutions. In this technical report, we investigate NbE in a typical setting, i.e. defining substitutions as operations. We show that this setting brings simplifications in proving syntactic properties and soundness of NbE, though complications are introduced in the completeness proof of NbE.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Language to Leverage Structure and Semantics at the LLM Interface
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
Textual Large Language Models (LLMs) provide a simple and familiar interface: a string of text is used for both input and output. However, the information conveyed to an LLM often has a richer structure and semantics, which is not conveyed in a string. For example, most prompts contain both instructions ("Summarize this paper into a paragraph") and data (the paper to summarize), but these are usually not distinguished when passed to the model. This can lead to model confusion and security risks, such as prompt injection attacks.
  This work addresses this shortcoming by introducing an LLM-native mark-up language, LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced "Lemon"), that enables the structure and semantic metadata of the text to be communicated in a natural way to an LLM. This information can then be used during model training, model prompting, and inference implementation, leading to improvements in model accuracy, safety, and security. This is analogous to how programming language types can be used for many purposes, such as static checking, code generation, dynamic checking, and IDE highlighting.
  We discuss the general design requirements of an LLM-native markup language, introduce the LLMON markup language and show how it meets these design requirements, describe how the information contained in a LLMON artifact can benefit model training and inference implementation, and provide some preliminary empirical evidence of its value for both of these use cases. We also discuss broader issues and research opportunities that are enabled with an LLM-native approach.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 28 pages

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Language-Based Agent Control
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: This paper introduces language-based agent control (LBAC), a new programming model for agentic applications that brings techniques from programming languages and language-based security to the problem of agent control. In conventional programming, combinations of static typing and runtime enforcement have long been used to guarantee that well-typed programs satisfy user-specified policies, including policies for access control, information flow, data provenance, and more. The key idea behind LBAC is to extend these guarantees to agentic applications by requiring agents to generate programs that are themselves well typed in the context of the surrounding scaffolding code. Unsafe programs are rejected by the type-checker before execution, allowing policies to apply uniformly across the entire application, including both agent-generated behavior and developer-written scaffolding. At the same time, LBAC preserves substantial expressiveness: agents may perform arbitrary side-effect-free computation and recursively invoke subagents, which retain full tool access subject to the same -- or potentially more restrictive -- policies. We demonstrate LBAC with three case studies: I/O sandboxing via filesystem capabilities, data provenance, and information-flow control.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: ANEForge: Python for direct computation on the Apple Neural Engine
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: ANEForge is a Python package that programs the Apple Neural Engine (ANE), the fixed-function neural accelerator on every recent Apple device, directly and without CoreML. In production the engine is reachable only through CoreML, which treats it as a scheduling option: no configuration requires the ANE, and a model can silently run on the CPU or GPU instead. ANEForge compiles a lazy tensor graph, built from 58 fused operators and 19 native bridge operators, into a single ANE program. The program is dispatched through the same ANE daemon and kernel-driver stack as Apple's internal framework. Beyond inference, the package reaches the engine's native fused attention, streams int8, int4, and sparse weights, keeps decoder and optimizer state resident across steps, and runs the forward pass, backward pass, and optimizer update of training on the engine. A small fused program completes a call in about 90us, near the engine's 70us per-program dispatch floor, and a pretrained ResNet-18 forward runs end-to-end in 0.33ms. ResNet-18, a sentence encoder, and a Vision Transformer run end-to-end against framework references, and a Stable Diffusion U-Net validates its forward pass. ANEForge targets Apple Silicon under macOS 14 and later. Each release is verified against a recorded macOS and ANE-compiler version.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 8 pages

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: When Double Rounding is Correct
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
Number libraries, which implement number formats and their arithmetic in software, are used to simulate hardware, making hardware behavior reproducible and thus verifiable and easier to design. However, modern machine learning accelerators are difficult to simulate, as they increasingly use specialized number formats that existing number libraries do not support. It is costly to extend these libraries using traditional methods: each combination of operation, format, and rounding mode typically requires a bespoke implementation. An easier way is to double round - compute at higher precision, then re-round - so that one high-precision kernel serves many formats, but double rounding is only known to be correct in select cases.
  We give a precise, efficiently checkable characterization of when double rounding is correct across many formats and rounding modes. Our result rests on a novel abstract number format that unifies fixed- and floating-point representations, reducing the correctness of double rounding to format containment: whether every value of one format is representable in another. We mechanized these results in Lean 4. In addition, we introduce a format inference algorithm that, given a sequence of operations, bounds each expression by a number format guaranteed to contain its result.
  We apply these insights in two ways. First, we present MPFX, a correctly-rounded, multi-precision number library that exploits correct double rounding to efficiently simulate many number formats. MPFX's correctly-rounded operations are up to 11x (mean: 6.05x) faster than MPFR's, and competitive with SoftFloat's - between 0.46x and 1.63x as fast (mean: 0.94x) - at the same precision. Second, in a case study, we implement a software simulation of a hardware specification using both SoftFloat and MPFX's primitives; the MPFX version is up to 13.5x faster.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Superset Decompilation
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Decompilation is the task of recovering high-level source from a compiled binary. Conventionally, it is implemented as a series of analyses and rewrites over a single representation, committing at each step to a single interpretation and discarding the rest. We argue this premature commitment is why decompilers struggle to produce compilable output on whole real-world programs, which is necessary for further testing. Compilation is many-to-one: a single binary may admit many source programs, and the evidence that resolves an ambiguity often lies far from where it arises. We therefore preserve competing interpretations when their resolution depends on non-local evidence, while resolving purely local ambiguities in a final solving stage. We formalize this approach as Superset Decompilation: monotone Datalog rules accumulate candidate interpretations across an IR hierarchy, and a per-function weighted MaxSMT solver jointly selects a globally type-consistent C program. Our implementation lifts stripped x86-64 Linux ELF binaries to C99 through CompCert IRs in 50K lines of Rust and Datalog. On GNU coreutils, it achieves 93\% recompilability and passes 7\% of the test suite.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: FDE-Gym: The Last Mile of AI Delivery
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Existing agent benchmarks typically evaluate agents on well-specified tasks defined by issue reports, specifications, or task tickets. Real-world customer delivery is different: forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) must clarify ambiguous requirements, work in live systems, and uncover unstated constraints. We introduce FDE-Gym, a benchmark of 95 end-to-end delivery tasks from 20 customer scenarios across 18 sectors, each adapted by industry experts from real-world delivery projects. In simulated customer environments with scripted stakeholders and modifiable customer systems, agents interact with stakeholders and operate on production-like systems to deliver working solutions. FDE-Gym scores a delivery by how much it improves the customer's own success metric, normalized between 0 (unchanged system) and 1 (reference solution), with penalties for stakeholder interactions (messages, trial runs, and waiting time). An online platform lets humans practice FDE skills under the same grading criteria. We evaluate 13 model configurations from seven providers. In the realistic setting, where unstated constraints must be discovered, the best configuration achieves a mean FDE-Gym score of 0.56 and resolves only 14 of the 95 tasks (a score of at least 0.8 with no incident). Discovering unstated constraints is the primary bottleneck: performance drops sharply when models must uncover them without explicit guidance. Yet information discovery alone does not account for the gap: even on the 23 tasks where the best configuration obtains every key fact from stakeholders, it reaches a normalized business uplift of 0.8 or above on only 10. These results reveal a substantial gap between solving well-specified tasks and delivering effective AI systems for real customers.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Are We Testing the Wrong Quantum Bugs? A Study of Fault Representation Gaps in Quantum Software Testing
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Quantum software relies on compilers, intermediate representations, and execution frameworks that transform programs before execution. Faults in these components can change the behavior of otherwise correct quantum programs. Yet quantum testing techniques are often evaluated using mutation-generated faults and curated bug benchmarks. We investigate how well the faults represented by these artifacts reflect those encountered in modern quantum software. We audit four quantum mutation-testing tools and three curated bug benchmarks, and collect 410 verified bugs from ten quantum software repositories over two years. We classify faults from all three sources into a common taxonomy of 56 bug families and compare their representation across mutation operators, curated benchmarks, and recent real-world bugs. The mutation tools support 20 bug families, and curated benchmarks add 15 more. Yet only 56 of the 410 real-world bugs (13.7%) belong to families represented by either source; the remaining 354 (86.3%) belong to families absent from both. The largest unrepresented families concern compiler transformations (66 bugs), type handling (53), and input validation (47). Unlike local gate or statement changes, these faults often depend on intermediate representations, compiler pipelines, input types, or dependency versions. Existing mutation operators primarily modify circuits and program constructs, whereas many real-world faults arise in the compilers, representations, and framework interfaces that process them. Addressing this gap requires looking beyond circuit-level faults toward testing semantic preservation across compiler transformations, correctness at representation boundaries, and interactions between software components. Our study provides empirical evidence to guide fault models and benchmarks that capture these mechanisms and preserve the contexts needed to reproduce them.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: WEAVE: Weaving Real-World Code Evolution into Dependency-Structured Tasks for Benchmarking and Training Code Agents
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Real-world software engineering rarely consists of isolated changes. Features, migrations, and systematic fixes often unfold across multiple pull requests (PRs), requiring coordinated modifications across a repository. Yet most executable repository-level benchmarks retain a single issue or PR as the task unit, while existing multi-PR settings rely on coarse aggregation and structure-agnostic evaluation. This mismatch obscures dependencies among changes and limits progress measurement and learning signals for long-horizon code agents. We introduce WEAVE, a framework that transforms verified PR histories into executable, dependency-structured tasks. WEAVE leverages repository-calibrated typed change loci to organize related PRs into bounded DAGs and instantiate each as a unified executable task. We further introduce Graph Credit, a deterministic, test-grounded metric that measures dependency-consistent partial progress and supports dense, verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning. Experiments on task construction, agent evaluation, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning show that WEAVE yields coherent executable tasks, enables more faithful progress measurement than flat scoring, and provides effective supervision and verifiable rewards for training code agents.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: RAG4Tickets: AI-Powered Ticket Resolution via Retrieval-Augmented Generation on JIRA and GitHub Data
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Modern software teams frequently encounter delays in resolving recurring or related issues due to fragmented knowledge scattered across JIRA tickets, developer discussions, and GitHub pull requests (PRs). To address this challenge, we propose a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework that integrates Sentence-Transformers for semantic embeddings with FAISS-based vector search to deliver context-aware ticket resolution recommendations. The approach embeds historical JIRA tickets, user comments, and linked PR metadata to retrieve semantically similar past cases, which are then synthesized by a Large Language Model (LLM) into grounded and explainable resolution suggestions. The framework contributes a unified pipeline linking JIRA and GitHub data, an embedding and FAISS indexing strategy for heterogeneous software artifacts, and a resolution generation module guided by retrieved evidence. Experimental evaluation using precision, recall, resolution time reduction, and developer acceptance metrics shows that the proposed system significantly improves resolution accuracy, fix quality, and knowledge reuse in modern DevOps environments.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Stateful Testing for Deep Learning Compilers
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Modern deep learning compilers compile models lazily and cache artifacts across invocations. Retained compiler state can make a later invocation incorrect even when it is correct in isolation. An analysis of 26 publicly reported issues in PyTorch, JAX, and TensorFlow shows that detecting such bugs requires sequences that first establish compiler state and then expose a failure. We present Rondo, a stateful testing method that represents each test case as a model paired with an invocation sequence. Rondo mutates invocation sequences and uses a Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler guided by compilation behavior to favor rarely observed behaviors. Its three-way differential oracle compares execution without compilation, compiled execution with compiler state reset, and compiled execution with state retained. It confirms stateful bugs by replaying the same invocation with state retained and reset while preserving inputs and program state, then shortens sequences while preserving the original bug. We evaluate Rondo on four deep learning frameworks using 24 common model architectures. Rondo detects 117 bugs, including 35 stateful bugs. We submit 39 bug reports, including 18 for stateful bugs; developers confirm 35 reports, including 16 for stateful bugs, and fix 18 bugs, including 11 stateful bugs. Rondo achieves the highest behavior coverage and compiler Python source-line coverage among the compared methods, with 99.26% alarm precision. It shortens 44 of 117 invocation sequences, reducing the lengths of these 44 sequences by 83.34% on average.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: ORACLE-SWE: Quantifying the Contribution of Critical Information Signals on SWE Agents
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Recent advances in Language Model (LM) agents have increasingly focused on repository-level software engineering (SWE) tasks, leading to various agentic workflows, training methods and failure analysis. Interestingly, rather than directly generating or evaluating edit patches, these approaches first examine and improve intermediate information signals collected during agent exploration, including Reproduction Test, Regression Test, Edit Location, Execution Context, and API Usage. Although different studies examine different subsets of these signals, no work has systematically compared their relative effectiveness in improving final task success or measured the remaining space for improvement in each signal. To address this gap, this work quantifies the contributions of both oracle and agent-extracted signals to final task success and measures the gap between current agent-found signals and their oracle counterparts. We hope our findings could suggest future research emphasis in SWE agents. We release our source code and oracle-signal dataset as a reusable methodology to benefit future signal analysis of SWE agents.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Enhancing Knowledge Density via Hierarchical Context Pruning for Retrieval-Augmented Repository-Level Code Completion
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has advanced repository-level code completion by retrieving external code snippets, API documentation, or type definitions to expand the model's contextual awareness. However, under the finite token budget of the context window, existing retrieval-augmented methods often saturate the budget with highly similar or even redundant code, which not only wastes tokens but also suppresses critical cross-file dependencies, preventing synergistic interaction between semantically similar reference snippets and cross-file dependency definitions. Therefore, further gains are limited by low knowledge density in the retrieved context rather than by model capacity. We propose SaraCoder, a retrieval-augmented framework that enhances knowledge density via hierarchical context pruning under a fixed context budget. A Hierarchical Feature Optimization module prunes an over-complete candidate pool in four stages. The freed tokens are then allocated to an External-Aware Identifier Disambiguator, which selectively injects only the most necessary cross-file dependency definitions. SaraCoder transforms context construction into a budget-aware optimization problem, balancing reference snippets and cross-file dependencies to build a context that is both knowledge-dense and semantically complete. Experiments on CrossCodeEval and RepoEval-Updated, across multiple backbone code LLMs, show that SaraCoder consistently outperforms strong RAG baselines such as GraphCoder and Repocoder in both code-level and identifier-level metrics, without increasing token usage, and yields synergistic gains when combined with other cross-file methods.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Benchmarking and Enhancing Design-Aware Code Review in the Linux Kernel
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
Code review often requires reasoning beyond local correctness. In mature software systems, reviewers must recognize design trade-offs introduced by a proposed change, compare alternative solutions, and reason about their compatibility with project-specific constraints. We refer to this problem as design-aware code review. However, existing automated review approaches primarily focus on defects and correctness, while the design knowledge accumulated in historical review discussions remains difficult to reuse.
  To address these challenges, we present DesignLore, a knowledge-augmented approach that extracts design decisions from historical review discussions, organizes them into an adaptive design taxonomy, and reuses relevant historical knowledge to guide code review. We further construct DesignReviewBench, a benchmark derived from real patch-review histories for systematically evaluating design-aware code review. Our evaluation shows that design-aware review remains challenging for current coding agents, with the strongest baseline achieving an F1 of only 0.213 on design trade-off detection. In comparison, DesignLore achieves an F1 of 0.259, a 21.6% relative improvement, and consistently delivers gains across different agent systems and backbone. These results highlight the importance of design-aware review and demonstrate the potential of recovering and reusing historical design knowledge to support it.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: SWE-Nexus: Automated Composition of Software Engineering Tasks from Test Execution
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Historical code changes provide convenient task boundaries, but do not identify which production functions selected tests exercise or support composing validated behaviors beyond a single change. We present SWE-Nexus, a fully automated pipeline that constructs repository-level implementation tasks from test execution. Four construction agents select tests, adapt tracing and evaluation protocols to each repository, and generate behavioral specifications. For each selected test file, tracing records an observed execution footprint of production function bodies. A scope is retained only if all expected scoring points pass in the original repository and masking the traced bodies causes at least one failure or error. Compatible scopes are composed deterministically, with shared functions counted once and every constituent test file revalidated under the complete combined mask. The benchmark contains 600 tasks from 105 repositories across six programming languages, including 116 atomic and 484 composite tasks. We evaluate 12 models under three agent scaffolds. The best configuration resolves 37.8% of tasks in one attempt, and scope-weighted scoring measures partial recovery. SWE-Nexus enables task construction from validated behavior beyond individual historical changes.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: CodeHealth Predicts the Token Cost of Agentic Code Review: A Pre-Registered Study of 465 Agent-Authored Pull Requests
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
Context: Organizations increasingly delegate code review to multi-agent large language model (LLM) pipelines billed per token. Low code quality raises human maintenance effort, but its effect on agent review cost has not been measured.
  Objective: We test whether baseline CodeHealth predicts the token cost of agentic review and fix beyond pull request (PR) footprint.
  Method: In a pre-registered observational study, we sampled 465 agent-authored PRs from 246 repositories in AIDev, jointly stratified by CodeHealth and footprint under repository caps. A frozen five-agent review-and-fix pipeline processed every PR with three different LLMs. Per LLM, we fitted a mixed model of log tokens on CodeHealth and log PR footprint, with a repository random intercept.
  Results: For all three LLMs the CodeHealth coefficient was negative, with 95% CI excluding zero; each CodeHealth point was associated with 3.5% to 6.1% lower token cost. CodeHealth was unrelated to PR footprint, so PR size does not explain the association. Two of three registered smells predicted fix cost; batch fixing left median CodeHealth unchanged. Exploratory analyses located the association in the review stage, where agents iterated more on unhealthy code without writing more comments. Adjusting for the size of the scored files absorbed the association, which we interpret as mediation by file size.
  Conclusions: A quality metric calibrated against human maintainability also predicts the inference cost of multi-agent review and fix. The effect is modest per point and not carried by PR size, so the refactoring case extends to agent-reviewed code when it changes structure and file size, not only the score.
  Data Availability: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22127920

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: NosRacer: Dynamic Detection of Race Conditions in On-Device Network Operating Systems
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
Commercial on-device network operating systems (NOSes) run the complex control planes of production routers and switches, where configuration update tasks are executed by multiple loosely coupled components through asynchronous message passing. Such executions are prone to race conditions: the same ordered input commands may produce different outcomes when messages are delivered in different orders. The race conditions are difficult to expose because they often manifest only as subtle, delayed malfunctions. Existing static analysis techniques lack scalability and precision for large-scale industrial NOSes, while dynamic ones incur substantial system-execution cost when attempting to cover the space of asynchronous message interleavings.
  To address the challenges above, we present NosRacer, a dynamic analysis framework for race condition detection in industrial-grade on-device NOSes. NosRacer uses a two-phase design. The concentration phase reduces analysis scope by leveraging the locality of configuration update tasks. Race condition detection is then limited to a small subset of involved components and crucial state variables, thereby reducing the detection cost. The perturbation phase proactively perturbs message asynchrony to increase the likelihood of executions with race-condition-exposing message interleavings. It keeps perturbation practical by grouping compatible perturbations for parallel execution and adaptively strengthening perturbations.
  We implement NosRacer in a commercial, actively developed NOS. NosRacer is integrated into the existing testing factory and used to detect race conditions in 5 key control-plane components. NosRacer achieves 66% precision and detects 21 race conditions confirmed by developers as severe bugs, while keeping the detection overhead below 10%.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: The Code of Theseus: Can Agents Rebuild Software from Recovered Design Documents?
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
LLM agents increasingly design a system before implementing it, yet the data to train and evaluate them centres on implementation and testing: requirements and design artefacts are often missing, outdated or private. Source code, in contrast, is abundant. Prior work recovers architecture documentation by feeding LLMs the source code or letting agents explore it, which saturates the context, does not scale to many repositories, and yields a single artefact rather than aligned ones.
  We present a framework that recovers aligned stakeholder intent, requirements and architecture from a compact repository representation, a static dependency graph and key contextual files, and release the artefacts of 10,764 Java, Python, C/C++ and C# repositories as a dataset. An LLM judge rates the artefacts of three generators as clear and internally consistent, but less reliably correct and at the right level of abstraction.
  To test whether the artefacts carry the design, we pose a software Ship of Theseus: a coding agent rebuilds 29 Commit0 libraries from the intent alone or with the recovered requirements and architecture, given only an interface contract and part of the tests. The artefacts do not significantly change the held-out pass rate (33.7% vs. 35.8%), but bring the rebuilt module structure significantly closer to the original (module F1 from 0.54 to 0.63), with either generator and even with concise artefacts.
  Recovered artefacts thus convey design that tests do not capture, offering a scalable source of design-level data for agents that design before they implement, and the round trip measures this without human references.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Don't Regenerate, Debug: A Domain-Specific Agent for Repairing Near-Miss Accelerator Kernels
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Kernel generation for hardware accelerators such as GPUs and NPUs has become a proving ground for large language models (LLMs), and state-of-the-art systems raise correctness through pipelines that couple LLMs with agentic reinforcement learning and evolutionary search. Such pipelines generate, compile, and execute large numbers of candidate kernels, discarding most of them and forgoing the opportunity to distill failures into reusable knowledge. Many discarded candidates are near-miss operators that compile and run but fail numerical validation; each embodies genuine domain knowledge and a nontrivial investment in LLM inference, cross-compilation, and hardware execution. We argue for a paradigm shift: rather than regenerate, debug. Debugging is far more constrained than generating from scratch: the search space is small and feedback is dense. We present a domain-specific debug agent that addresses three core challenges in autonomous repair: mitigating knowledge scarcity through retrieved patterns and diagnostic instrumentation, ensuring integrity through anti-cheat detection and full-coverage evaluation, and controlling cost via convergence guards and bounded iteration. Debugging serves two complementary roles: it extends the capability frontier by recovering operators that repeated regeneration fails to produce, and it lowers cost per deliverable operator. Debug Pass@1 achieves 66.7% versus Regenerate Avg Pass@1's 25.9% and Regenerate Pass@3's 40.7%, while consuming 92.8% fewer tokens per success than three-trial regeneration. Component ablations show that the knowledge base drives recovery, while integrity gates reject 12.5-33.3% of the successes the workflow itself accepted.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Smart Hiring Redefined: An Intelligent Recruitment Management Platform
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Against the backdrop of deepening digital and intelligent transformation in human resource management, traditional recruitment models struggle to fully meet enterprises' growing demand for precise talent acquisition due to limited efficiency, high costs, and information asymmetry. As a vital tool for optimizing recruitment processes, reducing labor and time costs, and enhancing core competitiveness, intelligent recruitment management systems have become an indispensable component of modern organizational talent strategies. Compared with the labor intensive tasks of resume screening, candidate position matching, and interview coordination in traditional manual recruitment, intelligent recruitment systems significantly enhance the efficiency and accuracy of the hiring process through automation and data driven approaches. These systems enable rapid parsing of massive resume volumes, intelligent matching of candidates to positions, and automated scheduling of interview processes. This substantially reduces the workload on human resources departments while improving recruitment quality and response speed. This research leverages the Java technology framework to design and implement an intelligent recruitment management system tailored for campus recruitment scenarios. The system establishes a collaborative platform connecting students, enterprises, and administrators through information technology and intelligent solutions, offering comprehensive functionalities including job posting distribution, resume submission, candidate position matching, and process management. Guided by the vision of Smart Campus Recruitment, the project delivers a more convenient job seeking experience for students and provides enterprises with more efficient talent screening and recruitment management services, thereby driving high quality development in university enterprise collaboration.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Realization Divergence in Multi-Provider Quantum Computing: A Pre-Registered Study of What Survives Measurement
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Quantum programs pass through compilers, transpilers and vendor services before execution. However, the distance between what was written and what runs is rarely measured. We call this distance realization divergence: the observable difference in how an identical source circuit is realized and behaves across quantum software stacks. We report a hardware study across three vendors and four devices, combining pre-registered predictions with explicitly identified exploratory analyses and amendments. In a compilation experiment with assigned placement policies, embedding radius correlates with two-qubit overhead at Spearman 0.805, against 0.492 for circuit size. Under a fixed lowest-index policy, an eight-qubit Bernstein-Vazirani circuit exhibits greater execution divergence than a twelve-qubit circuit on IQM Emerald. The opposite ordering occurs on IQM Garnet. Both comparisons replicate across two repetitions with disjoint confidence intervals. These results support a placement-dependent explanation, without isolating individual hardware noise mechanisms. The same ordering inversion is absent on the all-to-all IonQ control. On Rigetti Cepheus, a follow-up using topology-aware native placement found no consistent advantage in correct-answer probability for either submission track, but did not establish equivalence between the tracks. Structural comparisons depend on metric weighting, placement and device generation. Provider interfaces also limit observability: Rigetti's supported-operation list remained unchanged across a device generation that replaced the native entangler. We classify silent interface failures in composed toolchains and identify checks at toolchain boundaries, connecting valid cross-provider comparisons with concrete software-quality practices.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Spec-Driven Development as Prescribed and as Practiced
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: AI coding agents implement software from naturallanguage instructions, but the intent behind that work is lost when stated only in chat sessions. Spec-driven development (SDD) addresses this by having developers and agents write specifications that guide implementation, yet evidence on its use comes largely from tool vendors. We study SDD in practice through a thematic analysis of Reddit discussions, interviews with 21 practitioners, including eight tool makers, and 266 active and popular repositories in SpecMine, a corpus of 470,795 spec files from 73,030 public GitHub repositories that we release. Practitioners agreed that specs should capture intent, but many also included implementation details, used SDD selectively and mainly for new features, and reported more reliable agent behavior alongside greater planning and review costs. Our findings show that implementation detail may help agents while making specs prone to decay, that tool-specific record structures shape what people and agents see, and that participants described spec-code checks mainly when changes are completed rather than over time. We also find that individual benefits may come from clarifying intent before delegation, while team benefits may depend on SDD becoming a shared process. We derive implications for tool builders, practitioners, and researchers.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: GoLeash: Mitigating Golang Software Supply Chain Attacks with Runtime Policy Enforcement
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Modern software supply chain attacks consist of introducing new, malicious capabilities into trusted third-party software components, in order to propagate to a victim through a package dependency chain. These attacks are especially concerning for the Go language ecosystem, which is extensively used in critical cloud infrastructures. We present GoLeash, a novel system that applies the principle of least privilege at the package-level granularity, by enforcing distinct security policies for each package in the supply chain. This finer granularity enables GoLeash to detect malicious packages more precisely than traditional sandboxing that handles security policies at process- or container-level. Moreover, GoLeash remains effective under obfuscation, can overcome the limitations of static analysis, and incurs acceptable runtime overhead.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Praxist: From Experimental Artifacts to Solution Lineages
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Autonomous R&D agents now write, run, and improve executable artifacts under automated evaluation-but largely as laboratory instruments: shown on curated benchmarks, with gains that are hard to trace to a cause and costs well above what sustained engineering practice absorbs. The limitation is structural. Most systems treat each attempt as nearly self-contained, so logs, memories, and search trees record what happened without establishing which design element produced an improvement, whether its evidence survived validation, or how it recombines with others. Long campaigns therefore keep re-learning the same lessons. We introduce Praxist, a lineage-centered generational system that converts reproducible artifacts and evaluator outcomes into a typed evidence graph of findings, lane-structured frontiers, and agendas. Separating local artifact construction from cohort-level evidence synthesis lets later attempts inherit validated mechanisms, unresolved claims, and useful constraints, and leaves results attached to an inspectable lineage. On the standardized 75-task MLE-bench suite, the finalized official-grader results give Praxist 60 medals (80.0%), 49 of them gold, against 55 medals (73.3%) and 34 gold for a Claude Code baseline on Claude Opus 4.8-at a recorded model spend of $3054 versus $38370, roughly a twelfth of the cost. Five case studies-quantitative trading, LiDAR-inertial-visual SLAM, tokamak magnetic control, rocket landing, and job-shop rescheduling-carry the same process into open-ended engineering problems, improving on each task-native baseline in headline accuracy, survival, or resource cost, with the discovery path on record. Stronger artifacts at an order of magnitude less spend, each backed by an auditable lineage, are, to our knowledge, first brought together here: the operating profile production research requires, not the one a benchmark demonstration establishes.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Independent Data-Integrity Verification for LLM-Driven Functional Coverage Closure in Hardware Design
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: LLM agents can write directed tests that close functional coverage, but coverage only shows that a state was reached, not that the data on the way there was correct. This is a long-known point in verification and we do not claim it as new. We describe a small coverage-closure agent that applies it to an LLM loop: coverage is read from the report that the simulation itself exports (cocotb-coverage YAML) and never taken from the model's account, and data integrity is checked by scoreboards that are separate from the model. On three architecturally distinct RTL designs (an asynchronous FIFO, a UART transmitter and an AHB2APB bridge) the agent raised coverage from 91.7%, 88.9% and 67.4% to 100% within its 8-iteration budget in every logged run, using one design-agnostic agent. A reactive scoreboard monitor attached to the FIFO's base testbench also found a clock-domain-crossing bug in the author's own stimulus code. The monitor is not yet attached to the LLM-generated tests, so their data integrity is not independently checked; one manual check on a single FIFO test is reported as preliminary. We list the weaknesses of this evidence: three designs, no baseline, no ablation, and logged runs that come from several agent checkpoints.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Poison Valleys: Diagnosing Path-Dependent Failure in LLM Code Repair
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: When code-repair agents fail, final tests reveal that a patch is wrong but not which earlier commitment caused it or which software obligation failed. Poison Valleys traces this path in 1,844 model requests on two synthetic Python cases: PersistQueue adds atomic batch claiming to a disk-backed queue, while Dijkstra adds source-sensitive filtering to shortest-path search. We define plausible but incorrect software mechanisms, place each in a model's hypothesis, implementation plan, or both, and evaluate the generated code with an Oracle and targeted diagnostic coordinates. Moving the misconception from hypothesis to plan increased failure by 32.2% in PersistQueue and 28.9% in Dijkstra after matching the experimental mix. Different misconceptions produced distinct, model-dependent patterns of violated obligations, although several could converge on the same behavior. This creates a measured connection from upstream misconception to code mechanism and failure form. Code, data, and demo: https://poisonvalleys.org.
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.comment: Accepted to Interpreting Agent Behavior (IAB): The First Workshop on Human-Centered Interpretation for Understanding Agents, Humans, and Interaction (NeurIPS 2026 workshop); 22 pages; code, data, and demo: https://poisonvalleys.org

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: SWE-PolyVision: Benchmarking Cross-Image Abductive Reasoning for Repository-Level Software Engineering
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Current multimodal software-engineering benchmarks expose images as additional context, but do not test whether an agent can integrate evidence distributed across images into a verified repository-level repair. We present SWE-PolyVision, an executable benchmark of 92 real tasks from 36 open-source organizations, with 48 public tasks and 44 private holdouts. The release contains 402 static images and 6 videos, with at least two visual inputs per task. Each task pairs a fixed pre-fix repository with an isolated verifier and is evaluated under the supported conditions among three access modes: Text-only, Native Vision, and Tool-mediated Vision. Across eleven coding models, visual access changes which tasks are solved, but effects depend on both model and task. Two trace-linked Native Vision cases illustrate how complementary visual and textual clues can lead to source-localized, verified repairs; controlled interventions show that this conversion is not yet stable across inputs. SWE-PolyVision thus separates the availability of multi-image evidence from its successful use in repository-level repair, without treating patch success alone as proof of explicit reasoning.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: A Model-Centric DevOps Architecture for DEVS-Based Digital Twin Simulation Services
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Digital twin simulation models evolve and are redeployed like software. Engines based on the Discrete Event System Specification (DEVS) have a sound formal basis but offer little support for versioning, automated validation, or continuous delivery in cloud-native environments. This paper proposes a model-centric DevOps architecture that deploys DEVS-based digital twin simulations as managed services. Models are first-class DevOps artefacts written in a declarative language based on YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language) with a tuple-level mapping to the multiPDEVS formalism. Repository continuous integration (CI) validates publishing manifests, the engine loader performs syntactic, structural, and static semantic checks before every simulation, and published model artefacts are versioned and immutable, so that an earlier validated version can be selected by pinning its identifier. The platform runs as containerised microservices on Kubernetes with engine adaptations that externalise inputs and results and expose lifecycle control. An initial case study on bus route 22 in Riga exercises the lifecycle on an offline model with roughly 115,000 DEVS atomic components and reports single-container throughput and concurrent job execution on one Kubernetes node. Behavioural validation and multi-node evaluation remain future work.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: The Role of Agentic Instruction Categories for Code Generation: A Study of Five Python Libraries
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Agentic coding systems increasingly rely on repository-level agent files, such as AGENTS.md, to communicate project knowledge and developer intent. However, it remains unclear which categories of agent instructions enable efficient agent-file generation and accurate code generation. We evaluate five instruction categories: Repository Overview, Function Description, Implementation Detail, Testing, and Reconstruction Steps, across all 31 non-empty combinations using two Large Language Models (LLMs), Gemma 4 and GPT-5.4, and five human-written Python libraries. Our study addresses two research questions, comprising five sub-questions, on agent file generation and code generation. Results show that the number of instructions alone does not determine token usage for agent-file generation, with substantial variation across models and libraries. Although most AI-generated libraries compiled successfully regardless of the instruction combination, functional correctness remained limited. No Gemma 4 variant passed all tests, whereas 12.99% of GPT-5.4 variants did. Function Description achieved Gemma 4's highest partial-pass rate, while Reconstruction Steps achieved GPT-5.4's highest full-pass rate. For structural similarity to human-written code, Reconstruction Steps was most frequently associated with libraries closest to the originals in Lines of File and total Cyclomatic Complexity, while Testing and Reconstruction Steps were jointly most frequent for File Count and Function Count.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: ParanoiaEval: Benchmarking Unnecessary Defensive Work in Agentic Coding
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: As coding agents increasingly undertake real-world work autonomously, judging whether their risk treatments are warranted has become important. Existing work evaluates related agent behaviors from separate perspectives, but lacks a systematic framework for unifying these behaviors. To bridge this gap, we introduce ParanoiaEval, the first benchmark for unified evaluation of risk-treatment capabilities in coding agents. Grounded in the well-established Avoidance-Transfer-Mitigation-Acceptance framework in software engineering risk management, ParanoiaEval operationalizes its 4 fundamental treatments for coding-agent settings and contains 200 evidence-controlled repository-level task pairs, each differing only in treatment-defining evidence. We further introduce dedicated metrics for risk-treatment violations and evidence responsiveness, using a human-calibrated agentic judge for reliable evaluation. Large-scale experiments on 8 representative models and a post-hoc human study reveal that (I) unnecessary risk treatment occurs in 11.2%-58.7% of runs despite explicit evidence, with substantial variation across agent configurations; (II) stronger task capability does not ensure more appropriate risk treatment, while treatment violations substantially harm developers' experience, establishing risk treatment as an independent capability dimension; and (III) agents exhibit systematic patterns consistent with established risk-management findings, suggesting that knowledge from human practice can guide the diagnosis and improvement of this capability.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Evaluating and Improving Static Application Security Testing Tools for Rust
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Rust has become a popular systems programming language in recent years because of its strong guarantees on memory and concurrency safety. Many types of system software have been re-implemented in Rust. However, Rust programs can still suffer from common memory and concurrency vulnerabilities due to unsafe code and misunderstandings of its complex mechanisms. To mitigate such vulnerabilities, developers often rely on static application security testing (SAST) tools. However, the effectiveness of existing Rust SAST tools on real-world vulnerabilities remains underexplored. In this paper, we first conduct an empirical evaluation of mainstream Rust SAST tools using security vulnerabilities identified in real-world Rust applications. We systematically assess their effectiveness, uncover common weaknesses, and analyze the root causes behind them.
