Gecko-inspired dry adhesives provide a lightweight, passive, and residue-free solution for robotic capture in space, yet current systems operate in open loop, without the ability to estimate their own contact or adhesion state during interaction. This paper presents a real-time interaction-awareness framework that enables sensorized gecko-inspired adhesive interfaces to estimate their contact state throughout the adhesion lifecycle using embedded capacitive sensing. Five discrete interaction states (idle, proximity, contact, engaged, and disengaged) are classified using experimentally collected and augmented sensor data, enabling a comparative evaluation of six lightweight machine learning models suitable for embedded deployment. Among the evaluated models, Random Forest achieved the highest offline classification accuracy of 95.65%. For online deployment, combining Random Forest with a rule-based state machine improved accuracy from 78.02% to 93.14%, achieving a macro F1-score of 0.9343 while maintaining a 53 ms inference cycle. These results demonstrate that incorporating physics-consistent state constraints significantly improves robustness during realtime inference, representing a step toward interaction-aware capture in future autonomous orbital servicing missions.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: Physical AI: Concepts, Techniques, and Challenges
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: In recent years, physical artificial intelligence (physical AI) has experienced rapid development, capturing significant attention in academia and industry. However, the field has yet to reach consensus on its definition, technical landscape, and core challenges. To address this gap, this monograph seeks to define physical AI, present its technical landscape, and examine each key technical subfield in depth. In doing so, it establishes a unified framework for Physical AI: artificial systems that perceive, model, and act upon the physical world through continuous feedback under real-world constraints. Further, this monograph distinguishes physical AI from conventional digital AI, embodied AI, cyber-physical systems, and digital twins. It develops the foundations of physical AI across physics, control, cognition, learning, and reasoning. It reviews key methodologies, including multimodal perception, physical data and simulation, world models, embodied foundation models, motor-control systems, multi-agent coordination, and hardware-software co-design. Furthermore, it examines applications spanning robotics, manufacturing, infrastructure, scientific experimentation, and autonomous services. Particular attention is given to sim-to-real transfer, reliability, real-time execution, evaluation, safety, governance, and long-term deployment. By connecting perception, prediction, decision-making, action, and adaptation in a closed loop, this monograph identifies the technical challenges and research directions required to advance from narrow automation toward more generalizable physical AI and, ultimately, physical artificial general intelligence (Physical AGI).

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: ACE-Brain-0.6: Scaling Spatial Grounding for Physical Foundation Models
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: General-purpose multimodal models, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5, demonstrate broad capabilities in embodied manipulation. Our analysis indicates that this generality is accompanied by strong spatial perception, as Astra can determine where to interact with task-relevant entities amid visual distractors. Because spatial perception connects high-level reasoning to the physical scene, we investigate scaling visual grounding to strengthen the perceptual foundation of general embodied operation. We develop a unified data pipeline that combines robot manipulation recordings with complementary visual data from diverse sources. After automatically annotating the robot recordings, the pipeline converts the collected data into verifiable grounding supervision. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on approximately 1.5 million samples produced by this pipeline yields ACE-Brain-0.6. The model outperforms GPT-6 Astra on four of seven public grounding benchmarks, with an overall average score of 75.41 compared with Astra's 73.68. Under a fixed Qwen3.5-9B fine-tuning setup, aggregate grounding performance improves steadily as successive data releases expand the training collection to cover a broader range of grounding scenarios. These results show that scaling verifiable grounding supervision from diverse sources can strengthen the spatial perception of an open 9B model for general embodied operation.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: Embodied Playground: A Long-Horizon Agentic Robotics Benchmark for Physical, Strategic, and Spatial Reasoning
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: Foundation models offer a promising basis for robotic agents, but long-horizon tasks require them to sustain coherent reasoning and reliable physical execution across interdependent stages. We introduce Embodied Playground, a benchmark for evaluating how foundation-model agents coordinate physical, strategic, and spatial reasoning throughout such tasks. Agents must track task progress, satisfy intermediate constraints, and revise their plans using execution feedback as earlier actions shape subsequent decisions. The playground comprises 410 task environments spanning basic manipulation, sequential puzzles, and multi-stage household activities, with variations in planning depth, geometric constraints, and physical execution demands. We curate EP-100, a representative selection of 100 tasks across five suites and 16 task types, together with the EP-Easy and EP-Hard difficulty splits and the compact EP-20 selection. A shared protocol specifies observation and tool access, resource budgets, repeated trials, and independent checks of goal completion, task-rule compliance, and physical validity. Embodied Playground provides a unified framework for studying whether foundation-model agents can sustain effective reasoning and action over extended task horizons. https://winniechen2002.github.io/Agent-bench-website/

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: A Trust Ledger and an Execution Check for CPG-Based C-to-Lean 4 Autoformalization: Separating Declined from Silently Incorrect Translations
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: Verifying large C codebases requires translating them into formally checkable semantics, but most autoformalization work reports a single aggregate success rate that conflates two different failure modes: code the translator declined to handle and code the translator translated incorrectly. We present a deterministic code-property-graph (CPG)-based exporter that translates C source into a small Lean~4 core semantics under a three-tier correctness discipline: hole-free, call-closed, and dynamic-hole-risk, that keeps these modes distinct. Applied to a re-export of the SQLite source tree (8{,}602 functions, over 1.5~million AST nodes), the exporter translates 5{,}222 functions (60.7\%) hole-free, of which only 2{,}134 (24.8\%) are call-closed, a $2.4\times$ gap a single rate would hide. Both figures are reported in a full per-construct trust ledger rather than a single score. Our main contribution is methodological: a protocol for separating constructs that are fundamentally unresolvable by whole-program static analysis (such as public API boundaries) from constructs that only look that way. For example, we retracted our own ``impossible'' classification of function-pointer/vtable dispatch after tracing a concrete counterexample in the target codebase. Separately, a search for ``more holes closed'' surfaced a latent silent-wrong-answer bug: a translation that succeeded with an incorrect result rather than declining, a failure mode we argue is more dangerous than any hole, and one a hole-count-only evaluation would never surface.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 12 pages

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: VeGo: Direct Deductive Formal Verification of Go Programs for Computer Science Education
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: As formal methods are rapidly becoming accessible and practical due to AI coding agents, priority passes to assisting developers and students in generating specifications. Leveraging native HMX/SSA verifiers provide that support with rigorous mathematical guardrails. We present VeGo (Verified Go), a deductive formal verification system that enables direct verification of standard Go source code. VeGo incorporates Hoare-style contracts, loop invariants and integer variants, well-founded recursive measures, block-level scope invariants, and equational reasoning chains with primed variables directly as non-intrusive Go comments. We detail the language selection rationale justifying Go as an ideal balance over C, C++, Java, and Rust, strategically adopting Go's native multiple return values. We detail the tool architecture, exploiting the theoretical equivalence between Static Single Assignment (SSA) form and first-order functional programming to annotate code, desugar of clopen interval quantifiers, add Reynolds' skip statement, provide weakest precondition calculus, and native Hindley-Milner constraint inference, and verification condition resolution over the SSA form. We formalize contract-precision checking (weakest precondition vs. strongest postcondition) using an explicit analogy to type inference. Finally, we evaluate VeGo across educational textbooks and outline a roadmap for formal concurrency specifications using epistemic temporal logic.
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).comment: 12 pages + 4 pages appendix. Revised draft: reconciled benchmark data provenance, clarified gradual mode assume-after-assert discipline, and expanded related work

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: CrossTL: Hub-Based Translation of GPU Programs and the Preservation of Source Rules
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: GPU programs are written in vendor languages that disagree about integer overflow, division by zero, NaN handling, floating-point contraction, data layout and dispatch, so a translated program can compile and still compute something else. We describe CrossTL, an open-source translator that routes ten GPU source languages to eleven targets through CrossGL, a textual hub language, with repository-scale porting, contracts that loaders check, and native parity tests. We define faithful translation as refinement up to rejection under a compile configuration, and test whether a hub that records each source rule and lowers it through one per-target table keeps rules that a syntax-only hub loses. On an internally pre-registered suite of 66 hazard kernels in six languages, run on an Apple GPU through Metal, MoltenVK and WebGPU and on CPU implementations of Vulkan, OpenGL and an emulated Direct3D 12, SPIRV-Cross, naga, Tint, Slang and CrossTL each lose some source rule, and outcomes change with Metal's math mode and between two Vulkan implementations. A rule-carrying prototype of the hub removes 34 of 39 divergences on the rules it carries, against 14 for local fixes to four SPIR-V defects, and refuses where WGSL cannot express a rule. The registered hypothesis that it keeps every rule fails: MoltenVK, a non-conformant Vulkan layer, drops a rule that correct SPIR-V carries natively. On 2,585 programs written by third parties, 31% of CrossTL's translations are usable, established translators produce valid output significantly more often in 31 of 39 comparisons, and carrying the rules changes no target's accepted share by more than 0.2 points. Recording each operation's source rule suffices for the rules tested but is not necessary: one strongest rule would keep them too, at about nine times as many rewrites and 58 more refusals on the corpus.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: MOSAIC: More LLMs, Less Cost through Collaborative Reasoning for Compiler Optimizations
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: LLM-guided compiler optimization has recently shown promise. However, current LLM-guided optimizers query a single LLM at every search step, so their cost grows with both that model's price and the search budget. A smaller model is cheaper but degrades the search: in our experiments, a recent single-LLM optimizer reaches 10.2% (6.0%) lower speedup on GPU (CPU) with gpt-5-mini than with GPT-5.2. Agentic multi-LLM frameworks add controllers, concurrent calls, and shared memory, whose overhead can offset the savings of cheaper models. This paper shows that the optimization search tree itself can coordinate heterogeneous LLMs: the tree already records which proposals improved the program, and we can augment the tree to record which model made them. That evidence can then be used to decide which model should propose next. To this end, we introduce MOSAIC, in which each Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) node records a program and the LLM that expands it, and the active LLM proposes both a compiler transformation and the LLM for the next step. We also contribute an LLM-aware UCT that favors smaller models and a course-alteration rule that invokes the largest model only after repeated small-model regressions. Against that single-LLM optimizer run with GPT-5.2 alone and the same number of search iterations and tree parameters, on an NVIDIA GPU (Intel CPU), MOSAIC with eight LLMs improves the geometric-mean speedup on five kernels by 7.2% (14.4%) and the end-to-end Llama-3-8B speedup by 1.61x (1.41x), while reducing kernel compilation time by 1.95x (1.74x) and API cost by 4.47x (4.32x), with GPT-5.2 making only 23.1% (23.9%) of LLM calls. With the same eight models, random or round-robin model choice improves over the single-LLM baseline by only 2.5% on CPU, showing that the gains come from letting the LLMs choose the next model rather than from mixing the pool at random.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Structure-Aware Equivalence for Evaluating Autoformalized Statements
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary:
Evaluating autoformalized mathematical statements requires determining whether a candidate preserves the mathematical claim intended by a trusted reference. Existing methods approach this problem from complementary directions: reference-free learned evaluators estimate semantic agreement but are not constrained to a formal equivalence relation, while reference-based proof methods typically employ whole-statement logical equivalence to provide formal certificates, which is too coarse for translation fidelity and may identify mathematically unrelated statements.
  We introduce Structure-Aware Equivalence (SAE), a role-preserving formal equivalence relation between syntactic and whole-statement logical equivalence that allows formally justified reformulations while preserving translation-relevant mathematical structure. We operationalize SAE in the Autoformalization Correctness Evaluator (ACE), which provides certified equivalence or inequivalence judgments and reports Inconclusive otherwise. On ProofNetVerif, a benchmark introduced with BEq+, ACE retains substantial equivalent-case coverage while remaining highly conservative in certifying disputed or inequivalent pairs. On targeted diagnostics, BEq+ accepts 94-96% of unrelated but whole-statement logically equivalent pairs, while Mathesis LeanScorer accepts 42% of localized meaning-changing perturbations; ACE accepts none of either set as equivalent.

Programming Languages (Static Analysis).title: Conjugate Compilation: Self-Improving Agentic Co-Compilation for Speculative Decoding
Programming Languages (Static Analysis).summary: As LLM adoption surges, scaling model serving requires unlocking stranded GPU capacity alongside deploying more GPUs. Speculative decoding brings two models into the serving process: a small draft model proposes tokens that a larger target model verifies. Yet compiling these models individually leaves their shared execution outside the compiler's optimization boundary. We introduce CONJUGATE COMPILATION, which reframes speculative decoding as a cross-model compilation problem and jointly optimizes the draft and target models within their shared execution rather than treating each in isolation. Our key insight is that cross-model compilation should be informed by the measured performance of the co-located shared execution it produces: an optimization that improves a kernel in isolation need not improve the models when they execute together. To expand cross-model opportunities, we devise operand layouts that interleave blocks from both models within common tiles, co-locating GEMM and non-GEMM work while preserving their mathematics. We realize CONJUGATE COMPILATION through a self-improving agentic search system in which an LLM edits cross-model optimization plans using the compiler and GPU execution as its environment. Each proposed plan is compiled and evaluated through its co-located shared execution, whose measured score, together with kernel-level verdicts and compiler feedback, informs subsequent proposals, while Monte Carlo tree search accumulates rewards to guide exploration. Across six single-GPU speculative-decoding configurations on NVIDIA B300 and RTX 5090 GPUs, CONJUGATE COMPILATION achieves a geometric-mean per-round speedup of 1.37x over conventional execution. Interleaved kernels raise this speedup to 1.45x, reaching 1.59x in the best case. CONJUGATE COMPILATION also improves GPU utilization on average by 1.46x on RTX 5090 and 1.50x on B300.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Agentic Reverse Engineering: From I/O to Code with Discovery Agent
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: The automatic synthesis of a program from any form of specification is regarded as a holy grail of computer science. Fueled by LLMs, NL2Code has achieved tremendous success, yet the fundamentally more challenging task of synthesizing programs from input-output behavior, which we refer to as IO2Code, remains largely unsolved. Whereas NL2Code can exploit the semantic alignment between natural language and code acquired during pretraining, IO2Code requires recovering underlying principles from concrete computational behavior, navigating a vast and underspecified hypothesis space. To address this, we propose DIO-Agent, a discovery agent that performs agentic reverse engineering from input-output behavior to code. Our method frames IO2Code as an evolutionary search over discrete program space, in which an LLM serves as the mutation operator and concrete error signals from execution guide each mutation. To prevent the search from wandering into structurally complex yet incorrect dead ends, we introduce the Transformation Priority Premise as a mutation prior that biases the LLM toward the simplest hypothesis consistent with current evidence, progressively escalating from constants to conditionals to iteration only when simpler constructs are insufficient. To facilitate systematic study, we further construct an IO2CodeBench spanning multiple difficulty levels. Extensive experiments show that DIO-Agent consistently outperforms both traditional program-by-example method and SOTA evolution-agent baselines across all difficulty levels and various LLMs, while substantially surpassing test-time scaling strategies with equivalent sampling budgets.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: VReAct: Verification as an Architectural Layer for LLM Agents: A V-Model Design, and a Pilot Study of Its Deterministic Core
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents built on the ReAct pattern concentrate four responsibilities in one model: selecting a strategy, choosing each action, formatting it, and judging whether the result is adequate. Nothing outside the generative loop can reject its output, so an agent that cannot progress does not report failure; it runs until an external budget terminates it. We propose VReAct, which treats verification as an architectural layer for ReAct agents by adapting the software-engineering V-model: specification levels descend from requirements to individual steps, each paired with a dedicated verifier; a deterministic controller enforces every verdict; and only verification outcomes write memory. A rejection thus localizes the level that introduced the fault, and an agent halts by declining rather than by exhaustion. Each verifier separates a zero-cost deterministic gate from an optional LLM judge, so the contribution and cost of each can be measured independently. A pilot study implements the acceptance- and unit-level verifier pairs, comparing five configurations that share one executor, tool set, and scorer and differ only in verification components, on the four-hop stratum of MuSiQue with an 8B-parameter backbone. Across 47 executions, the two unverified configurations answered none of ten questions, every run ending at a step cap or provider token limit; the verified configuration without a planner answered eight of ten and abstained on the rest. Deterministic gates produced eight of nine observed corrections at zero marginal cost, and planning degraded performance once verification was present. These results characterize termination behavior, not accuracy at scale; we outline a twelve-month plan to complete and evaluate the full architecture, including the integration-level pair the pilot omits.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: From Software History to Executable Regression Tasks: A System for Evaluating Software Agents
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: As software agents increasingly generate and modify code, evaluating their ability to review changes and discover defects becomes important. Such evaluation needs executable project environments for investigation and reliable defect references supported by reproducible behavior. Existing code review benchmarks provide limited support for this combination. We present a system that constructs executable regression instances from historical introducing--fixing commit pairs and developer tests. The system extracts candidate tests from fixing-side changes, then uses constrained agents to transplant them and configure version-specific environments while preserving production code and test expectations. Independent replay and evidence-based review verify whether tests that fail on the introducing version and pass on the fixing version support the proposed regression relationship. Accepted instances retain both versions' replay recipes, validated tests, and execution evidence. Repair-supported analysis and human review add root-cause locations, tested repairs, and causal explanations. These instances support bug detection and localization in code review, and enable bug repair and regression-test generation on the same defects. The system constructs 172 validated instances from 522 candidates across 11 Python projects. We evaluate three software agents with ten models and additional reasoning-effort settings on 83 manually selected, enriched instances across the three tasks. Precise root-line localization remains challenging, while baseline combinations achieve repair and regression-test generation success rates of up to 68.7% and 77.1%, respectively. Leading configurations differ by task, and higher task performance does not necessarily yield greater API-cost efficiency. Our approach provides reusable executable evidence for studying agents' defect discovery, repair, and testing capabilities.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Beyond Similarity-Based Generation: Guiding Commit Message Generation with Issue-Commit Traceability
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Commit messages provide records of code changes and help developers understand and maintain software. To reduce the manual effort involved in writing them, commit message generation (CMG) approaches automatically generate commit messages that describe code changes in natural language. Existing CMG approaches generally treat CMG as a standalone task and optimize generated messages primarily for similarity to developer-written references. However, this objective may not properly reflect the practical usefulness of generated commit messages. This limitation matters in current AI-assisted software engineering workflows, where commit messages are used as shared information to serve different software engineering activities. To fill this gap, we propose TraceMsg, which uses issue-commit traceability, a representative software engineering activity, to guide commit message generation. TraceMsg is a collaborative multi-agent framework that coordinates message generation, traceability reasoning, and feedback-guided refinement, allowing generated messages to serve traceability while using reasoning feedback to guide issue-conditioned refinement. We evaluate TraceMsg on six open-source projects. The experimental results show that TraceMsg achieves an average Hit@1 of 0.893 and an MRR of 0.911, improving Hit@1 and MRR by 13.16% and 38.75%, respectively, over the best baseline for each metric.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Noise-Awareness in Quantum Software Testing: An Empirical Landscape Analysis
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) hardware has transformed quantum computing into a practical experimental platform while introducing fundamental challenges associated with hardware noise, decoherence, and probabilistic execution. Although quantum software testing (QST) has rapidly emerged as an active research area, it remains unclear to what extent existing testing methodologies explicitly engage with noisy and hardware-constrained execution environments. This paper presents a systematic empirical landscape analysis of noise-awareness in QST research through a deterministic, taxonomy-guided analytical framework applied to 61 papers published between 2018 and 2025 across eight testing paradigms, contrasting how contributions are framed with how they are evaluated. Among the analyzed papers, 47 (77.0%) are noise-oblivious and only 14 (23.0%) explicitly engage with noise-related execution concerns, while only 11 (18.0%) report evaluation on physical hardware or a noisy simulator. Test generation, the largest paradigm, exhibits a noise-awareness rate of only 14.3%, and debugging and repair 18.2%; coverage-based, metamorphic, and differential testing contain no noise-aware contributions. Noise-aware methodologies emerged late and remain outnumbered in all analyzed years. Framing and evaluation are strongly associated (odds ratio 40.5, p < 0.001) yet diverge for individual papers: 5 of the 14 noise-aware papers evaluate only on ideal simulators. Inferential statistical tests are reported in only 16.4% of papers. The classification framework was validated against a blinded, human-coded reference sample, achieving almost perfect inter-rater agreement on testing-technique classification and substantial agreement on noise-awareness. The framework provides a reusable empirical basis for longitudinal analysis of hardware-conscious testing practice.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Zero2Repo: Can Coding Agents Build Repositories from Scratch?
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Coding agents are increasingly asked to build software rather than patch it, yet benchmarks for from-scratch repository construction are mostly limited to a single language and depend on manually curated tasks. We introduce Zero2Repo, a benchmark in which an agent receives a product requirements document, an interface contract, and an empty workspace, and must deliver a complete repository in the project's native ecosystem. Tasks are produced by a language-agnostic authoring pipeline that converts real, version-pinned open-source projects into behavioral specifications, reproducible environments, and hidden acceptance tests. Each task is validated by execution: a reference implementation derived from the upstream project must pass, and adversarial validation must show that the tests reject incorrect implementations. Evaluation runs production coding agents in isolated containers, withholds the acceptance tests until an explicit submission, and assigns a binary reward only when every test passes, with no LLM judge. The pipeline and harness make no language-specific assumptions and apply to mainstream programming ecosystems; the current release contains Python, TypeScript, Go, and C++ tasks. Even on 11 tasks drawn from repositories that frontier models have very likely seen during training, the strongest agent solves only 10, and every failing submission passes 90-99% of the hidden tests; for the two strongest agents, 67-100% of failed tests trace to a single omission or a low-frequency rule stated in the specification rather than to a missing subsystem, so each failure is a concrete target for improvement.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Automated structural testing of LLM-based agents: methods, framework, and case studies
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: LLM-based agents are rapidly being adopted across diverse domains. Since they interact with users without supervision, they must be tested extensively. Current testing approaches focus on acceptance-level evaluation from the user's perspective. While intuitive, these tests require manual evaluation, are difficult to automate, do not facilitate root cause analysis, and incur expensive test environments. In this paper, we present methods to enable structural testing of LLM-based agents. Our approach utilizes traces (based on OpenTelemetry) to capture agent trajectories, employs mocking to enforce reproducible LLM behavior, and adds assertions to automate test verification. This enables testing agent components and interactions at a deeper technical level within automated workflows. We demonstrate how structural testing enables the adaptation of software engineering best practices to agents, including the test automation pyramid, regression testing, test-driven development, and multi-language testing. In representative case studies, we demonstrate automated execution and faster root-cause analysis. Collectively, these methods reduce testing costs and improve agent quality through higher coverage, reusability, and earlier defect detection. We provide an open source reference implementation on GitHub.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Many Repairs, One Direction: Steering Code Models Toward Safer Cryptographic API Use
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Cryptographic API misuse in large language model-generated code can compromise software security. While many existing approaches improve code security by modifying model parameters or inputs, how representation changes associated with different cryptographic API repairs can support a shared intervention for safer code generation remains underexplored. To investigate this, we construct 48,000 matched program pairs across four programming languages and ten cryptographic API misuse categories. Each pair changes a specified API decision while preserving the programming task. Subtracting the misuse program's internal representation from its secure counterpart's gives a repair vector. Across five models, comparisons of mean repair vectors reveal stronger organization by misuse category than by language. These category-specific patterns also support a shared intervention. We introduce CrypSteer, which extracts a shared direction by normalizing repair differences and selecting a principal component aligned with repairs across misuse categories. With model weights fixed, adding one shared direction per model to its internal activations during generation improves aggregate target security rates by 5.28--15.00 percentage points over unsteered generation across languages and misuse categories. These findings connect the shared structure of cryptographic repair representations to a reusable intervention for safer code generation.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Which Code Changes Need Re-embedding? CIPBench and the Limits of Multi-Signal Index Maintenance
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
Repository-level retrieval-augmented generation systems must keep vector indexes synchronized with continuously evolving code, yet there is no principled basis for deciding which changed code units actually need new embeddings. We ask whether the retrieval impact of a code change can be anticipated before that embedding is computed.
  Across 10 open-source repositories in Python, Go, and JavaScript, we characterize how a change propagates from syntactic substantiality through embedding displacement to retrieval impact. The links are informative but not deterministic: syntactic class separates displacement sharply, yet impact depends on a unit's retrieval exposure as much as on how far its representation moves, and recurring counterexamples bound what any single signal can decide. We formalize the decision as CIPBench, a benchmark that scores maintenance policies under a strict pre-embedding information boundary.
  Prediction works, and one signal exhausts it. A ranker using only a unit's change history substantially reduces retrieval harm relative to random and recency-based scheduling. Combining it with three further signals--individually discriminative and largely unassociated with one another--leaves the decision statistically unchanged across every budget we evaluate, for reasons we trace to the structure of the score rather than to its tuning. What pays off is not ranking but filtering: units whose text is unchanged from the indexed state can be skipped with no risk and, in the most reversion-heavy project, at nearly half the embedding cost. Signal-level informativeness is therefore not evidence of decision-level value, and separating the two requires evaluating the decision a signal produces rather than its association with the outcome.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: OpenCollab: A Multi-Agent Coding Framework with Programmable Collaboration and Controllable Runtime
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Multi-agent coding systems are designed to tackle complex software engineering tasks through collaboration. However, existing evaluations typically assume configured organizations are followed faithfully, whereas reality differs. This behavioral gap, combined with differences in underlying system components, prevents clear attribution of observed gains. To this end, we introduce OpenCollab, a multi-agent coding framework that provides a unified infrastructure for programmable collaboration and controllable runtime. Specifically, OpenCollab unifies organization design, enforces experimental control on a shared runtime, and tracks execution through fine-grained event streams. On this basis, we define Adherence to quantify whether the declared organization is actually realized. Our experiments reveal that agents collaborate very differently across configurations: changing any single dimension shifts Adherence, from 47.2% to as high as 97.2%. Furthermore, extensive agentic coding benchmarks show that OpenCollab (Duo) establishes new SOTA performance compared to the mainstream harnesses such as Mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, Codex CLI, and Claude Code, showing that a well-designed organization can outperform strong existing harnesses, while OpenCollab's single-agent configuration uses the fewest tokens across all evaluated suites. OpenCollab establishes a unified multi-agent infrastructure for easy programmable collaboration and controlled causal evaluation.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Over-Defense in Coding Agents Begins at Silent Forks
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Language models behind coding agents are post-trained with outcome rewards, and recent methods concentrate credit on the turns that decide the outcome. We find that defensive actions beyond what a task requires escape both. They begin at silent forks, the turns where every next action leads to the same outcome. Such actions leave the success rate unchanged, and frontier models take the disproportionate branch there in up to 91% of decisive actions under implicit budgets. The most direct fix, a checker in the trajectory reward, reaches these forks only through fully proportionate trajectories, leaving 74% of GRPO groups with identical rewards and behavior unchanged. This motivates a rethink of where learning signals belong, namely where behavior diverges, which a behavioral checker can locate and the outcome cannot. Our method, ForkDPO, contrasts a proportionate and a disproportionate action at the same prefix, at silent forks on both sides of the required behavior. On a test set of unseen repositories, it lowers a 4B model's disproportionate behavior from 70.3% to 58.9%, against 67.7% for DPO at randomly chosen turns, establishing behavioral divergence as a learning signal for how agents act beyond whether they finish. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Astarojth/silent-forks.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: The Complexity Kink: A Prompt-Side Structural Complexity Index for Code-Generation Reliability
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Measuring complexity from a model's own code is biased by failure: a hard prompt can produce a short, broken program that looks simple. We instead score each prompt's structure on six dimensions from the prompt alone, never from generated code or test results. We draw 5,000 Python prompts across six bands of a preliminary single-rater score, and four out-of-panel LLM judges rescore every prompt (composite ICC(2,1) = 0.872). Twenty-one models answer every prompt (105,000 generations), and an independent LLM auditor, checked against known-answer cases, reviews each unit-test verdict. Averaged over models, pass rate has a nonmonotone breakpoint at composite 14.0: 83.4% at or below, 90.1% above. That jump is not a law of difficulty: with task-type fixed effects the breakpoint stays at 14.0 but the adjusted jump shrinks from 6.8 to 0.4 points, and neither of the benchmark's two prompt sources reproduces it on its own. Nineteen models pass more often above their own breakpoint and two less often; one of those declines comes from API calls that returned nothing. In post hoc follow-up, Kimi K2.5 shows the clearest decline, at 14.25, under a prompt-source control and within the later source alone. Among failed generations with measurable output complexity, 25.0% pair a prompt composite above 8 with output complexity of at most 10, twice the share among passing ones. The pooled breakpoint moves to 11.25 on raw test outcomes. Human agreement with the index is moderate, paraphrase and cross-language rescoring preserve its ordering, and overidentification tests reject the six dimensions as instruments, so we make no causal claim. The contribution is a prompt-side way to locate where each model's pass rate changes and to test how much that depends on the prompt mix and on how success is scored.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Theory of Developer Momentum: The Developer's Experience of Progress and the Craft of Maintaining Motion
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: This paper introduces a Theory of Developer Momentum that helps us see the activity of developing software in motion and the skilled craft through which progress unfolds. We define Developer Momentum as the developer's experience of progress and forward motion toward the goal of a task. Our theory disentangles the related constructs of flow state, momentum, and motivation, so we can more clearly see the relationships between them and how they interweave to support progress. In order to make progress, developers build up working context in memory, become immersed in a cognitive puzzle, and gain clarity through motion in uncertain terrain. The theory provides researchers with a rich experiential lens to investigate how developers' cognitive experiences are shifting in emerging AI workflows. Building on prior grounded theory work, we conducted in-depth interviews with a theoretically sampled subset of 12 professional developers, and eight feedback interviews to evaluate resonance and investigate how the theory translates to agentic AI workflows. We followed a Constructivist Grounded Theory approach to construct a theory grounded in empirical data. Our theory contributes a novel paradigm for seeing the motion of developing software at multiple scales and resolutions, seeing the living capacities that support this motion, and expanding what becomes available for improvement, skilled judgment, and craft.

Security & Program Analysis.title: SoK: Systematizing LLM Prompt Security: Taxonomies, Datasets, and Unified Evaluation of Attacks and Defenses
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Prompt-security claims for large language models (LLMs) are often compared as properties of individual attacks or defenses, although measured harmfulness depends on the target model, access setting, attack and defense configuration, prompt sample, and judger. We systematize 272 studies through three linked, multi-label taxonomies of jailbreak attacks, defenses, and model vulnerabilities. To make these dependencies explicit, we introduce an access-compatible evaluation protocol over configured $\langle M,A,D,S,J\rangle$ tuples and instantiate it in PromptSecurity, an open-source platform that records method settings, outputs, judgments, and query costs. We release two complementary datasets: JailbreakDB, with 445,752 jailbreak system-user prompt pairs and 1,094,122 benign prompts, and PromptSecurity-Eval, with 166,200 harmful-query and 25,800 benign-utility output records. We evaluate 11 target models, 20 attacks, nine defenses, and three automated judgers under a matched, single-turn protocol using 100 harmful queries and separate benign-utility tasks. Lower attack success can reflect failure to execute transformed requests rather than stronger safety; attack-category advantages can reverse when one method is excluded, and attack success varies with assistant choice. Defenses can reduce harmful outputs while degrading benign-task utility or causing backfire. Rejudging identical outputs also shows that measured attack success is sensitive to the behavior supplied to the judger, highlighting the need to report judger configurations alongside ASR. These findings motivate configuration-aware reporting rather than context-free method rankings.
  Resources: https://datasec-lab.github.io/PromptSecurityLeaderboard/ https://huggingface.co/datasets/youbin2014/JailbreakDB https://huggingface.co/datasets/youbin2014/PromptSecurity-Eval https://github.com/datasec-lab/PromptSecurity

Security & Program Analysis.title: Cerium: A Multi-GPU Framework for Terabyte-Scale Encrypted Inference
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Encrypted AI using fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables inference directly over encrypted queries, providing strong privacy guarantees. However, its computational and memory overheads have limited practical deployment. Custom FHE accelerators improve performance, but rely on advanced manufacturing technologies that limit their accessibility. GPUs offer a more widely available alternative, yet achieving ASIC-class performance on GPUs is challenging. Large models such as LLMs compound these challenges by requiring optimized kernels, terabyte-scale memory management, and efficient execution across multiple devices.
  We present Cerium, a multi-GPU framework for large-scale FHE inference. Cerium combines a domain-specific language, an optimizing compiler, and a runtime system to automatically generate optimized GPU kernels, compress plaintext data, manage terabyte-scale memory footprints, and optimize multi-GPU communication.
  Implemented on NVIDIA GPUs, Cerium outperforms expert-written GPU libraries by up to 2.25x and achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art FHE ASICs, matching the CraterLake ASIC. It is the first GPU system to execute CKKS bootstrapping in under 10 milliseconds, achieving 7.5 milliseconds, and is the first to demonstrate encrypted inference for BERT-Base and Llama3-8B prefill in 8 seconds and 43 seconds, respectively. The Cerium framework is open-source and available at https://github.com/CMU-CAOS/Cerium
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 18 pages

Security & Program Analysis.title: A Trust Ledger and an Execution Check for CPG-Based C-to-Lean 4 Autoformalization: Separating Declined from Silently Incorrect Translations
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Verifying large C codebases requires translating them into formally checkable semantics, but most autoformalization work reports a single aggregate success rate that conflates two different failure modes: code the translator declined to handle and code the translator translated incorrectly. We present a deterministic code-property-graph (CPG)-based exporter that translates C source into a small Lean~4 core semantics under a three-tier correctness discipline: hole-free, call-closed, and dynamic-hole-risk, that keeps these modes distinct. Applied to a re-export of the SQLite source tree (8{,}602 functions, over 1.5~million AST nodes), the exporter translates 5{,}222 functions (60.7\%) hole-free, of which only 2{,}134 (24.8\%) are call-closed, a $2.4\times$ gap a single rate would hide. Both figures are reported in a full per-construct trust ledger rather than a single score. Our main contribution is methodological: a protocol for separating constructs that are fundamentally unresolvable by whole-program static analysis (such as public API boundaries) from constructs that only look that way. For example, we retracted our own ``impossible'' classification of function-pointer/vtable dispatch after tracing a concrete counterexample in the target codebase. Separately, a search for ``more holes closed'' surfaced a latent silent-wrong-answer bug: a translation that succeeded with an incorrect result rather than declining, a failure mode we argue is more dangerous than any hole, and one a hole-count-only evaluation would never surface.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 12 pages

Security & Program Analysis.title: Privacy-preserving Machine Learning in Internet of Vehicle Applications: Fundamentals, Recent Advances, and Future Direction
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Machine learning (ML) in Internet of Vehicles (IoV) applications enhanced intelligent transportation, autonomous driving capabilities, and various connected services within a large, heterogeneous network. However, the increased connectivity and massive data exchange for ML applications introduce significant privacy challenges. Privacy-preserving machine learning (PPML) offers potential solutions to address these challenges by preserving privacy at various stages of the ML pipeline. Despite the rapid development of ML-based IoV applications and the growing data privacy concerns, there are limited comprehensive studies on the adoption of PPML within this domain. Therefore, this study provides a comprehensive review of the fundamentals, recent advancements, and the challenges of integrating PPML into IoV applications. We first review existing surveys of various PPML techniques and their integration into IoV across different scopes. We then categorize IoV applications into three key domains and analyze the privacy challenges in leveraging ML in these application domains. Building on these fundamentals, we review recent advancements in integrating various PPML techniques within IoV applications, discussing their frameworks, key features, and performance in terms of privacy, utility, and efficiency. Finally, we identify current challenges and propose future research directions to enhance privacy and reliability in IoV applications.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Preprint

Security & Program Analysis.title: Redefining Hybrid Blockchains: A Balanced Architecture
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Blockchain technology has completely revolutionized the field of decentralized finance with the emergence of a variety of cryptocurrencies and digital assets. However, widespread adoption of this technology by governments and enterprises has been limited by concerns regarding the technology's scalability, governance, and economic sustainability. This paper aims to introduce a novel hybrid blockchain architecture that balances scalability, governance, and decentralization while being economically viable for all parties involved. The new semi-centralized model leverages strategies not prevalent in the field, such as resource and node isolation, containerization, separation of networking and compute layers, use of a Kafka pub-sub network instead of a peer-to-peer network, and stakes-based validator selection to possibly mitigate a variety of issues related to scalability, security, governance, and economic sustainability. Simulations conducted on Kubernetes demonstrate the architecture's ability to achieve over 1000 transactions per second, with consistent performance across scaled deployments, even on a lightweight consumer-grade laptop with resource constraints. The findings highlight the system's scalability, security, and economic viability, offering a robust framework for enterprise and government adoption.

Security & Program Analysis.title: DECKER: Domain-invariant Embedding for Cross-Keyboard Extraction and Recognition
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Acoustic side-channel attacks (ASCA) on keyboards pose a significant security risk, as keystrokes can be inferred from typing acoustics, revealing sensitive information. Prior ASCA studies are limited by small-scale datasets with restricted diversity in users, keyboards, and environments, constraining analysis across devices, microphones, and noise conditions. We introduce HEAR, a dataset designed to study ASCA along three axes: keyboard generalization, noise adaptation, and user bias. HEAR contains recordings from 53 participants using 37 laptop keyboards, collected in three realistic settings: (1) external microphone capture, (2) device microphone capture without network noise, and (3) VoIP-based streaming capture. This enables controlled evaluation across users, keyboards, and environments. On HEAR, we establish an ASCA benchmark spanning conventional features and pre-trained representations from raw audio and spectrograms in unimodal and multimodal settings. We propose DECKER, a domain-invariant keystroke inference framework with four stages: (1) Keyboard Signature Normalization to reduce device coloration, (2) domain-adversarial disentanglement to suppress keyboard identity, (3) supervised cross-keyboard contrastive alignment to enforce key consistency, and (4) Acoustic Style Randomization to synthesize unseen keyboard responses. We further explore sentence-level inference using an LLM-based post-processing layer to refine keystroke sequences via linguistic context. Results on HEAR show DECKER improves keystroke identification over strong baselines, particularly in cross-keyboard and cross-user settings, with further gains from language-model rectification. These findings highlight that ASCA remains effective across diverse users, devices, and noisy environments, underscoring its practical security risk.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Accepted to AsiaCCS'26

Security & Program Analysis.title: Multi-Criteria Routing for Cryptographic Key Exchange in QKD Networks: Survey, Taxonomy, and a Conceptual Optimization Framework
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) networks enable unconditionally secure key exchange using quantum mechanical principles. However, routing cryptographic keys across multi-hop quantum networks introduces challenges unique to quantum communication. This survey analyzes and classifies 26 routing strategies proposed between 2013 and 2024 for terrestrial, satellite, and hybrid QKD infrastructures. Dynamic, key-aware routing algorithms have been shown to reduce service rejection rates by 25-40% compared to static shortest-path methods by incorporating real-time key pool availability and link error rates. Multi-path strategies improve resilience against trusted-node compromise by distributing keys across disjoint routes, albeit with an increase in key consumption of 30-60%. SDN-based orchestration frameworks emerge as essential enablers of flexible, QoS-aware routing for hybrid networks integrating terrestrial fibers and intermittent satellite links. Critical research directions include reducing dependence on trusted nodes through quantum repeaters or post-quantum cryptography, developing standardized key management interfaces for interoperability, and adopting AI-driven predictive routing for adapting to fluctuating network states. This comprehensive synthesis of routing algorithms, performance trade-offs, and unresolved issues offers practical guidance for engineering secure, adaptable, and large-scale QKD networks capable of meeting real-world deployment demands.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Adaptive Cyber-Defense for Evolving Attacker Capabilities using Reinforcement Learning and Behavior Trees
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Autonomous cyber-defense agents trained using reinforcement learning (RL) are increasingly adopted for defending enterprise computer networks. However, existing approaches may become brittle as attacker capabilities evolve and enable new attack strategies. In this work, we study the problem of adapting defender policies learned in CAGE Challenge Scenario 2 (CC2), a benchmark enterprise network defense scenario, to an extended network scenario with new attacker capabilities represented by new attacker actions. Effective attack strategies that leverage new actions are initially unknown, and therefore attacker policies must be learned before defender adaptation can occur. To address this challenge, we develop adversarial RL (ARL) with behavior trees (ARLBT), which uses reward behavior trees (RBTs) to define progression-based reward functions and condition attacker policies on RBT execution. The proposed RBT incorporates the new attacker actions into structured attack strategies while leveraging parallel execution to generate rewards across multiple network nodes simultaneously. We evaluate ARLBT for learning attacker policies against two baseline defender policies across network scenarios with different sets of new attacker actions and compare against multiple attacker baselines. The results demonstrate that ARLBT improves attacker success compared to ARL using the original CC2 reward function and that conditioning policies on RBT execution can improve sample efficiency. We further show that defender policies can be adapted against the learned attackers, improving robustness to attacks that leverage new attacker actions.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Spectrum of Liability: Forensically Sound Acquisition of Wireless Evidence for the Reconstruction of Maritime Cyber-Physical Incidents
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Modern maritime navigation depends on mandatory wireless inputs, most notably GNSS and AIS, whose reception can be spoofed or jammed. When groundings or collisions occur, liability and safety investigations often turn on whether RF interference corrupted bridge instruments, yet the artifacts typically available (VDR outputs, IBS logs, screenshots, decoded messages) are downstream, lossy, and easy to contest in adversarial proceedings. We introduce a forensically sound acquisition methodology that preserves upstream wireless evidence together with the minimal contemporaneous context needed to interpret it. Our system records coherent, multichannel IQ across relevant bands while simultaneously collecting time-aligned receiver and instrument-state metadata (e.g., decoded AIS/GNSS outputs and NMEA sentences), enabling later re-decoding and physical-layer reanalysis tied to what the onboard stack indicated at the time. To make the record independently auditable, we package samples and metadata into a single append-only forensic envelope that cryptographically binds per-stream hash chains with trusted-time anchors and periodic checkpoints, allowing third parties to detect tampering (modification, truncation, splicing, cross-case substitution) and to verify the claimed recording window. A prototype implementation shows the approach is practical: integrity mechanisms add negligible storage overhead and modest compute cost at operationally relevant multiband capture rates.

Security & Program Analysis.title: SEAL: Towards Persistent Tool Poisoning Attack against LLM Agents via Prefix-Eliciting Trigger
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Tool poisoning has emerged as a critical security threat to LLM agents, where adversaries embed malicious instructions in tool descriptions or external resources that enter the agent's context, allowing adversaries to manipulate agent's tool selection process. However, existing tool poisoning attacks primarily rely on an idealized assumption that the attacks task effect within a single interaction round. We show that their effectiveness degrades sharply in realistic multi-round agentic settings. We further reveal that this degradation stems from the fact that agents do not consistently surface attack-relevant signals in their reasoning as the planning context evolves, thereby weakening the attack's influence across rounds. To investigate whether tool poisoning remains a practical threat in such realistic settings, we propose SEAL, a two-stage method for persistent tool poisoning. Specifically, SEAL first performs Prefix-Eliciting Trigger Optimization (PETO) to optimize context-specific triggers that elicit attack-relevant reasoning prefixes, improving effectiveness within individual contexts. It then applies Local-to-Universal Trigger Aggregation (L2U) to combine these local triggers into a single universal trigger, improving generalization across different contexts and execution rounds. Extensive experiments across seven representative multi-round scenarios and different models demonstrate the attack effectiveness of SEAL, its transferability across target models, and its resistance to potential defenses.

Security & Program Analysis.title: GreenNIDS: A Benchmark Workflow and Analysis Dataset for NetFlow Intrusion Detection Experiments
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Comparing the predictive performance and computational cost of flow-based intrusion detection experiments requires both quantities to be available for each run. GreenNIDS connects benchmark execution on public NetFlow datasets to a reusable analysis dataset. Model implementations write a common set of outputs, which are ingested into a run-level table with companion tables for model configuration, feature importance, and training history. The run-level table combines predictive metrics with timing, throughput, memory use, and energy estimates based on thermal design power. A CPU-only demonstration comprises 216 runs across four dataset families, three versions, and binary and multiclass tasks. Ingestion produces a 216 x 96 analysis table with no duplicate run identifiers and complete Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) and F1 coverage. Multiclass ROC-AUC is missing for 36 PyTorch runs, making metric availability an explicit part of subsequent comparisons. The stored records support grouped performance and training-time plots, as well as resource screening after execution. Combining task-specific MCC thresholds with limits on training time, peak RAM, and estimated training energy retains 25.0% of the full run collection. These results establish compatibility within the evaluated collection and support comparisons after execution, subject to the recorded preprocessing, execution profile, and approximate energy accounting.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at IE 2026 (International Conference on Informatics in Economy)

Security & Program Analysis.title: On Pearl Blockchain's Proof of Useful Work: Systematization and Flexibility
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
We revisit the proof-of-useful-work (PoUW) scheme in Pearl blockchain's white paper (Pearl Research Team), giving a systematic sensitivity characterization as an alternative to its Jackpot policy, along with efficient algorithm for verifying the sensitivity condition.
  Beyond its independent interest, our characterization yields a more flexible PoUW scheme that eenables miner autonomy: each miner can independently choose its noise magnitude to tailor the trade-off between computational accuracy and mining efficiency to its own needs.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Equivalent Non-linear Shift Register Transformations and Espresso
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
The stream cipher Espresso was designed by E. Dubrova and M. Hell as a hardware-efficient candidate for 5G security. It has two components - a 256-bit binary non-linear feedback shift register (NFSR), with 14 feedback taps, and a 20-variable non-linear output function. However, the security of Espresso with regard to several standard cryptanalytic attacks are estimated using an alternate NFSR, which has only two feedback taps. The above analysis is based on the claim that this alternate NFSR is obtained using a transformation algorithm which preserves the output sequence of the original NFSR. This issue has become all the more significant in the light of recent results on hardware performance evaluations, which assume that the stated equivalence holds.
  This article presents the first successful attempt in settling the above question of Espresso NFSR equivalence. We arrive at our main result by a careful analysis of existing transformation methods relevant to the question. In doing so, we first identify and correct a critical flaw in the proof of a foundational result of E. Dubrova. Next, in the context of Espresso equivalence, we analyze and unify the transformation framework of Dubrova and the one proposed by Yao and Parampalli. Based on our analysis, we have succeeded in transforming the LFSR in an Espresso-equivalent design reported by Yao and Parampalli to the Espresso alternate NFSR. Further, we have obtained a corresponding non-linear output function which achieves output-equivalence with the LFSR design, and hence, with Espresso.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Estimating the Social Cost of Corporate Data Breaches
Security & Program Analysis.summary: While the size of a data breach is typically measured by the number of (consumer, customer, or user) records exposed or compromised, its economic impact is generally measured from the point of view of the corporation suffering the data breach: cost in crisis management, legal fees, drop in stock price, and so on. This study examines whether it is possible to estimate the true cost, or the social cost of a data breach, measured by the impact on its victims and their out of pocket costs. To accomplish this we establish: (1) the estimation of the average direct financial losses of an identity theft (IDT) victim, including the opportunity cost of lost time, and healthcare expenditures associated with distress associated with identity theft; and (2) the estimation of increases in incidents of IDT that can be attributed to a major breach event. Our findings show that the average social cost per victim has declined significantly since 2016. Furthermore, we find that there is indeed a statistically significant increase in the number of IDTs following a mega-breach event when accounting for a discovery lag of 1-2 months post-breach. Applying our model to real-world cases allows us to estimate an upper and lower bound social cost of specific mega-breach events. We find that for the 2009 Heartland and 2013 Target breaches, even the conservative lower bound social cost estimate exceeded settlements by factors of 5 and 16, respectively. In contrast, the 2017 Equifax breach resulted in a lower bound estimate of $263.8 million, falling well within its $700 million settlement cap. While the Equifax upper bound estimate of $1.72 billion in social cost more than doubles this settlement, the narrowing gap between institutional liability and an incident's social cost provides empirical evidence of a market saturation effect that reduces the marginal damage of individual compromised records over time.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Accepted to WEIS 2026

Security & Program Analysis.title: AdaFedXplain: Adaptive Federated Learning with Explainable AI for Ransomware Detection
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Attacks using ransomware have developed into complex multiphase campaigns that target vital infrastructure, resulting in annual damages of billions of dollars. Conventional detection techniques are ineffective against zero-day variations, and privacy issues are raised by centralized machine learning algorithms. Federated learning allows for cooperative model training without data sharing, however current FL approaches suffer from explainability issues, high communication cost, and non-IID data heterogeneity. In this study, we present AdaFedXplain, an explainable AI-based adaptive federated learning system for ransomware detection. Our approach includes progressive XGBoost complexity to avoid overfitting, a decaying learning rate schedule for stable convergence, and dynamic client grading based on ransomware prevalence and data sufficiency. Using 62,485 real-world ransomware samples from four OS-based non-IID clients, we compare AdaFedXplain against FedAvg, FedProx, and SCAFFOLD. According to experimental data, AdaFedXplain outperforms all baselines with 99.59% detection accuracy and 99.64% F1-score while cutting energy usage by 75%, latency by 65%, and communication overhead by 75%. The ablation investigation demonstrates that every element enhances performance. Security analysts can use SHAP explainability to identify important PE header characteristics that influence detection decisions. Our system provides a collaborative ransomware detection solution that is efficient and interpretable, while reducing privacy risks through federated learnings data-local training paradigm.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: https://nsclab.org/ml4cs2026/ (Eighth International Conference on Machine Learning for Cyber Security (ML4CS 2026) )

Security & Program Analysis.title: PRICE: Privacy-Preserving Image Classification in Mobile Edge-Cloud Computing with Homomorphic Encryption
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Cloud-assisted image classification enables many mobile AI applications, but transmitting raw images to the cloud raises significant privacy concerns. Homomorphic encryption (HE) allows computation over encrypted data; however, existing end-to-end HE-based inference pipelines incur prohibitive latency and computational overhead, limiting their feasibility for latency-sensitive mobile systems. This paper addresses how to enable efficient encrypted image classification in mobile edge-cloud environments without sacrificing accuracy. We propose PRICE, a three-tier edge-cloud architecture that partitions deep neural network inference between a trusted edge and an untrusted cloud. The edge performs lightweight feature extraction in plaintext, while only compact embeddings are encrypted using the Cheon-Kim-Kim-Song (CKKS) scheme and offloaded to the cloud for encrypted final-layer inference. This design avoids homomorphic evaluation of deep backbone layers, significantly reducing computation depth, ciphertext size, and end-to-end latency. To further improve efficiency, we develop RowHyDiag, a row-packed hybrid diagonal encoding with hoisted-rotation-aware encrypted matrix-vector computation, which minimizes rotation operations and improves slot utilization. Extensive experiments on real devices across five datasets demonstrate that, under the evaluated 128-bit-security configurations, RowHyDiag achieves up to 31.8$\times$ faster cloud inference, 85.3$\times$ fewer rotations, and 83.0$\times$ lower setup payload than the conventional Halevi-Shoup diagonal method. RowHyDiag also outperforms the PEGASUS linear-transformation baseline, providing 1.1-4.5$\times$ faster cloud inference and 1.2-3.4$\times$ lower setup payload. The results show that PRICE enables deployment-ready, low-latency encrypted inference for mobile edge-cloud systems under a trusted-edge threat model.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Federated Learning for Malware Image Classification under Data Heterogeneity
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Malware image classification (MIC), in which binary files are converted into visual representations and deep neural networks are trained to identify malware families, has recently emerged as an effective approach for malware detection. Federated learning (FL) enables malware image classifiers to be trained collaboratively by multiple clients without sharing raw data. However, a fundamental challenge in FL is data heterogeneity (non-IID), which is particularly relevant but understudied in the malware context. In this paper, we address this gap via three contributions. First, we present an empirical study of federated MIC under varying degrees of data heterogeneity across three popular malware image datasets (MalImg, Virus-MNIST, and MalNet). We show that while FL achieves strong accuracy under IID conditions, both accuracy and training stability degrade as data becomes increasingly non-IID. Second, we introduce a set of round-level statistics that characterize the data contributed by participating clients in each FL round, and demonstrate that class entropy (diversity of class labels present in a given round) exhibits strong positive correlation with global model accuracy. Third, leveraging this insight, we propose an entropy-aware client selection strategy that filters candidate client subsets based on class entropy, and show that our strategy outperforms standard random selection. Our results highlight the role of client composition in federated MIC and underscore the importance of distribution-aware classifier training under data heterogeneity.

Security & Program Analysis.title: SemVideoSte: Agentic AI for Cross-Modal Semantic Video Steganography Communication
Security & Program Analysis.summary: We propose an agentic artificial intelligence (AI)-driven cross-modal semantic video steganography communication (SemVideoSte) scheme for secure cross-modal information transmission. Agentic AI interprets the service context to determine a semantically matched public prompt and coordinates video generation, message embedding, semantic transmission, and message recovery process. A multi-mask mechanism combines variational autoencoder (VAE) reconstruction robustness, semantic transmission robustness, and latent separability to select reliable embedding positions. Meanwhile, a private digital token controls the random seed and guidance offset to construct positive and negative terminal latent states, enabling coverless message embedding during the final diffusion sampling step. Simulation results on open-source datasets demonstrate that SemVideoSte achieves high embedding capacity, reliable message recovery, and strong semantic consistency under different channel conditions. In addition, eavesdroppers without the correct digital token cannot reliably recover the secret message, and the generated stego videos effectively resist the steganalysis detection. We further establish a prototype testbed to verify the practical feasibility of SemVideoSte.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 13 pages, 11 figures

Security & Program Analysis.title: Can Trustless Agents Be Trusted? An Empirical Study of the ERC-8004 Decentralized AI Agent Ecosystem
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
As autonomous AI agents increasingly transact across organizational boundaries, a fundamental trust challenge emerges: how can an agent assess whether an unknown counterpart is trustworthy? The ERC-8004 protocol addresses this challenge with the first permissionless trust layer for AI agent economies, built around three on-chain registries for Identity, Reputation, and Validation. Despite its rapid adoption, the protocol has not been studied empirically, leaving it unclear whether the information it records provides a trustworthy basis for decision-making. To address this gap, we present the first empirical study of ERC-8004 across three chains: Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain (BSC), and Base, covering the period from protocol deployment through May 13, 2026. We crawl on-chain Identity and Reputation events, off-chain files, and x402 payment transactions.
  On the identity side, we find that most registrations are placeholders rather than active agents, with only a small fraction (3%, 4%, and 15% across Ethereum, BSC, and Base) exposing a valid ERC-8004 registration file with at least one live service endpoint. On the reputation side, we show that the Registry, as currently deployed, cannot function as a trust signal: values are not commensurable, feedback records are rarely grounded in verifiable interactions, and reputation can be manipulated at minimal cost. Consistent with these design weaknesses, we find that a substantial fraction of reviewers (73.5%, 59.2%, and 90.6% across Ethereum, BSC, and Base) exhibit coordinated Sybil behavior. After removing Sybil-flagged feedback, 15.8%, 77.9%, and 86.8% of rated agents, respectively, are left with no valid feedback. We then turn these findings into concrete recommendations for future revisions of ERC-8004. Our study yields actionable protocol-design implications and establishes an empirical baseline for research on AI agent markets.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Many Repairs, One Direction: Steering Code Models Toward Safer Cryptographic API Use
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Cryptographic API misuse in large language model-generated code can compromise software security. While many existing approaches improve code security by modifying model parameters or inputs, how representation changes associated with different cryptographic API repairs can support a shared intervention for safer code generation remains underexplored. To investigate this, we construct 48,000 matched program pairs across four programming languages and ten cryptographic API misuse categories. Each pair changes a specified API decision while preserving the programming task. Subtracting the misuse program's internal representation from its secure counterpart's gives a repair vector. Across five models, comparisons of mean repair vectors reveal stronger organization by misuse category than by language. These category-specific patterns also support a shared intervention. We introduce CrypSteer, which extracts a shared direction by normalizing repair differences and selecting a principal component aligned with repairs across misuse categories. With model weights fixed, adding one shared direction per model to its internal activations during generation improves aggregate target security rates by 5.28--15.00 percentage points over unsteered generation across languages and misuse categories. These findings connect the shared structure of cryptographic repair representations to a reusable intervention for safer code generation.

Security & Program Analysis.title: STRAL: What Adaptation Gains, Loses, and Costs in SOC Alert Screening
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Security-alert screening must balance false-alert burden against missed important events, yet adaptation can change which events are detected. We investigate this trade-off using STRAL, a score-triggered active-learning controller combining ADWIN monitoring, selective label acquisition, and bounded model updates, with an optional historical validation Guard. Across four chronological alert-stream settings, we compare adaptive screening with a fixed, non-adapting baseline (Frozen), measuring recall, false-alert burden, detection preservation, and label-query costs. On two AMiner settings, STRAL reduces false positives by 21.4% (14 to 11) and 16.7% (6 to 5), respectively, while preserving all Frozen detections. On Wazuh, Guard reduces false positives by 9.8% (522 to 471), while losing two Frozen detections. On NAD-CD, STRAL raises recall from 36.11% to 40.29%, but loses 40.1% of Frozen detections while gaining 3,000 others; false positives increase by 151.2%. Guard preserves Frozen decisions on NAD-CD but requires 3,550 label queries, compared with 2,000 for STRAL. These findings demonstrate why adaptive SOC screening must be evaluated through detection preservation, false-alert burden, and feedback cost alongside aggregate recall.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 8 tables. v2: PACT renamed STRAL to avoid a naming collision. Substantially revised model selection, threshold calibration, and empirical evaluation, including AMiner, Wazuh/AIT-ADS, NAD-CD, Guard, detection turnover, acquisition comparisons, classifier transfer, and sensitivity analyses. Security & Program Analysis.title: How Much Feedback Is Needed to Break Template Protection? The Geometric Vulnerability of Biometric Authentication
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Biometric authentication systems increasingly use privacy-preserving mechanisms to protect sensitive templates. However, the authentication interface itself may still leak information that enables reconstruction attacks. Prior attacks exploit released similarity scores, whereas more advanced systems reveal only the binary accept/reject decision. This binary feedback provides substantially less information, making template reconstruction far more challenging.
  In this work, we introduce query-efficient reconstruction attacks under extremely limited feedback, addressing two key limitations of prior attacks. First, we introduce the first attack that reconstructs protected biometric templates using only authentication success/failure feedback by exploiting the geometric constraints of biometric authentication. Second, we introduce distribution-aware query-efficient reconstruction methods for score-releasing systems, achieving a more realistic threat model by reducing the number of required queries by a factor of $5\times$ compared to recent prior score-based attacks. Finally, we combine these two insights by incorporating a pretrained facial diffusion prior into our geometric binary attack, reducing the number of required queries by a factor of $5\times$.
  Our findings reveal a fundamental security limitation of biometric authentication: independently of the template protection mechanism, the authentication process itself exposes geometric information that can enable perfect template reconstruction up to numerical precision. Moreover, the distribution of biometric templates can be leveraged to make significantly more effective reconstruction attacks.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: preprint

Security & Program Analysis.title: Cutting the Fuse: Actionable APT Attack Blocking in Provenance-based IDS
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Provenance-based Intrusion Detection Systems (PIDS) are a critical line of defense against Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs). However, their practical deployment is crippled by alert flooding; state-of-the-art PIDS focus on detection performance, outputting thousands of low-information, unactionable alerts.
