Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Directed Symbolic Execution for Vulnerability Discovery: An LLM-Guided Approach in KLEE
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Symbolic execution effectively discovers security violations but suffers from path explosion. Engines like KLEE therefore use path prioritization heuristics to order state exploration, typically optimizing code coverage. However, path prioritization can become trapped in cyclic control-flow regions, where repeated branching consumes the exploration budget before exploration reaches vulnerable code beyond these cyclic regions. We propose KLEECopilot, a Large Language Model (LLM)-guided directed symbolic execution approach built on KLEE. KLEECopilot uses LLMs to mark potentially vulnerable code and guide path prioritization. It also integrates loop-exit prioritization to escape potentially non-vulnerable cycles and progress toward deeper vulnerabilities. Compared with baselines such as Empc, KLEECopilot improves basic block coverage by 42.24% and line coverage by 125.82%. It discovers 1,335 total violations and 87 unique violations, outperforming the second-best baseline by 32.2% in total violations and Empc by 24.3% in unique violations. Although KLEECopilot is sensitive to model family, it exhibits only marginal sensitivity to model scale, supporting the efficacy of integrating security semantics and loop-exit prioritization. Ablation studies further show that individual components contribute to effectiveness: alternative configurations involving searchers, internal components, marking sources, and prompt variants yield only 54--61 unique violations, while KLEECopilot maintains competitive code coverage.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: When Code Becomes an LLM Call: An Empirical Study of Call-Site Contracts in Agentic Systems
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Software quality has long rested on specifications that state what code must do, and on testing and verification that check that the code does it. Agentic systems change this foundation: they replace parts of their logic, such as choosing the next tool, judging whether an action is allowed, or writing code to run, with calls to a large language model (LLM). The program still relies on what this logic must guarantee, but the model's behavior is not fixed by code, varies across runs, and can be steered by its input. The guarantee must therefore come from the program around each LLM call site, as a contract of pre-conditions, prompt constraints, and post-conditions. We present an empirical study of these contracts in 496 LLM call sites of 40 popular open-source agentic systems (13.4 MLOC, four languages). Using a multi-agent pipeline validated by 17,428 human judgments, we trace where every model output flows, derive an expected contract for each call site without access to its code, and compare it with the contract that the code implements. We find that 48% of LLM outputs reach control flow or execution, and 73% of these never reach a person. Programs enforce 78% of their constraints in code, but in the prompt, 67% of the constraints are only requested from the model. Although 82% of call sites are checked before and after the call, 63% of the expected constraints are unmet and only 5.3% of call sites satisfy their whole contract; ten recurring patterns explain 99% of the gaps. 38 mechanisms behind these gaps trigger at runtime, and a small code fix that enforces the expected constraint stops all 38. Our results show that the presence of checks says little about their adequacy, and we derive implications for agent developers, framework maintainers, and researchers.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Combining LLM and Dynamic Analysis for Universal Testing of Static Application Security Testing Tools
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Static application security testing (SAST) tools help detect potential software vulnerabilities, but they themselves contain faults undermining reliability and usability. Automated testing can address these issues, yet current techniques suffer from limited program transformation diversity and lack mechanisms to verify generated variants, leading to reduced fault detection and high manual effort. We present LLM4SAST, the first universal framework detecting faults in SAST tools using large language models and dynamic feedback. Our key insight is leveraging LLMs to understand and transform code in diverse programming languages. We design novel metamorphic relations with transformations to guide variant generation, using an LLM to produce multi-language variants that satisfy these relations. To reduce erroneous variants and identify unique faults, we propose two heuristics: dynamic-feedback-driven selection and program-differencing-based clustering. For each metamorphic relation, a report-centric test oracle detects variants that fail tests and identifies underlying faults by differentially analyzing SAST reports of the seed program and its variants. LLM4SAST identified 66 unique faults across six SAST tools, with 32 confirmed or fixed after being reported to developers, demonstrating effectiveness. The proposed heuristics eliminate 47.8% of false positives, and LLM4SAST detects 3.4 times more faults while requiring only 39.8% of the variants compared to existing approaches.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Evaluating and Improving Static Application Security Testing Tools for Rust
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Rust has become a popular systems programming language in recent years because of its strong guarantees on memory and concurrency safety. Many types of system software have been re-implemented in Rust. However, Rust programs can still suffer from common memory and concurrency vulnerabilities due to unsafe code and misunderstandings of its complex mechanisms. To mitigate such vulnerabilities, developers often rely on static application security testing (SAST) tools. However, the effectiveness of existing Rust SAST tools on real-world vulnerabilities remains underexplored. In this paper, we first conduct an empirical evaluation of mainstream Rust SAST tools using security vulnerabilities identified in real-world Rust applications. We systematically assess their effectiveness, uncover common weaknesses, and analyze the root causes behind them. Motivated by the study, we propose TRUST, a large language model (LLM)-assisted automated testing framework. TRUST automatically analyzes the official Rust reference to derive and implement semantics-preserving transformations. It leverages these transformations to generate mutant programs for evaluating Rust SAST tools and uncovering potential faults within them. Overall, TRUST has revealed 46 faults across six popular SAST tools, 17 of which have been confirmed. In addition, our study yields ten empirical findings and four practical lessons that provide actionable guidance for developing more effective, robust, and maintainable Rust SAST tools.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Backend-Frontend Converter: Component-Based Conversion of .NET Computational Models to TypeScript
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Computational models developed in .NET often need to run locally within web applications. We present Backend--Frontend Converter, an architecture for generating TypeScript implementations of component-based models. The converter maps components, connections, aliases, and formula trees to model-specific TypeScript code. Reusable runtime libraries provide numerical integration, data access, and state handling. We evaluate stored generated implementations through four orbital scenarios and a recorded trading-strategy comparison. Orbital calculations execute in a browser and are paired with C\# results by crossing event and timestamp; trading outputs are aligned by date. Analytic scheduler tests and deliberately perturbed outputs assess the validation procedure. Each orbital scenario produces 91 paired events with identical timestamps. Position and velocity differences remain below $(10^{-6}\)~km$ and $(10^{-9}\)~km/s$. All 20 analytic scheduler checks pass, and the comparator detects each of three prescribed state and time perturbations. The trading comparison contains 501 aligned daily records with matching indicator values, positions, and order events. The evaluated implementations preserve the compared outputs across the C#/TypeScript boundary. Component-specific generation and reusable execution libraries provide a practical route from supported .NET computational models to TypeScript applications.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Effective Construction of Feature Database of Fingerprinting Functions for Code-Clone SCA
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary:
In contemporary software development, the extensive adoption of third-party libraries has become standard practice to avoid reinventing the wheel. This trend is particularly evident in programming ecosystems that lack mature package managers, such as C/C++. Within this context, Code Clone Detection (CCD) techniques have emerged as essential tools for identifying instances of code reuse, thereby mitigating security and legal concerns. Despite significant advances in CCD algorithms, a notable gap persists between academic tools and real-world applications. This disparity primarily arises because academic tools rely on experimental datasets composed of a limited number of indexed repositories, whereas real-world applications require a much broader scope of code sources.
  To address this challenge, we propose a novel, systematic approach for selecting appropriate open-source repositories to construct a more effective CCD feature dataset. Our method, OSSScope, employs a greedy algorithm to analyze the diversity of fingerprinting functions across 2.55 million C repositories on GitHub, maximizing unique fingerprinting functions while minimizing the number of repositories required. OSSScope compiles an optimal feature dataset containing 61 million fingerprinting functions from 190K repositories, resulting in a 22.65% improvement in recall over SOTA tools, and covers over 95% of the features from other sources. Leveraging the selected repositories, we introduce RClassifier, a lightweight classification model that determines whether a repository should be included, streamlining construction for migration to other language ecosystems. Our evaluation of RClassifier in the Golang ecosystem validates its effectiveness, achieving recall comparable to the dataset produced by OSSScope.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Safety Analysis of CPSs Over-the-air Updates: Test Case Prioritization and Selection
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Over-the-air (OTA) updates for Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) allow engineers to modify their software wirelessly. In the automotive domain, they enable manufacturers to update software without physical access to the vehicle. However, OTA updates can generate a large number of possible software configurations. For example, end users may decide whether or not to install any given OTA updates. The combinatorial explosion of these configurations hampers SW testing, a standard practice for detecting errors in CPS. To overcome this limitation, we propose CRISP (CRIticality-based Selection and Prioritization), a novel framework supporting test case prioritization and selection in the context of OTA updates. Our framework leverages test case robustness, i.e., how far they are from violating the system requirements, to drive test case prioritization and selection. It enables engineers to rank test case executions from most to least critical, and to select only the critical test cases relevant to a given OTA update. We evaluated our approach using a representative SW product line consisting of seven different vehicles, 22 driving scenarios, and two software components. We considered 224 tests, requiring 59 hours of execution time. We assessed the effectiveness of CRISP across five OTA updates. We compared our solution with (a) a random test case prioritization and selection algorithm, and (b) AP-DISC, identified as the state-of-the-art solution in a recent empirical study on the subject. Our results show that CRISP outperforms our baselines in finding failure-revealing test cases, and that our selection procedure can be configured to find reasonable and practical tradeoffs among accuracy (percentage of failure-revealing test cases identified) and computational time (time required to find them).

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: Bridging Generation and Training: A Systematic Review of Quality Issues in LLMs for Code
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Large language models (LLMs) frequently generate defective code, ranging from logical bugs to security vulnerabilities. Training-data quality is one contributor to these outcomes alongside model architecture, optimization and alignment, prompting and inference context, and decoding. However, the literature connecting specific training data quality issues to observable generated code quality issues has not been synthesized systematically. We review 114 included papers and establish taxonomies of eight generated-code quality dimensions and two broad groups of training-data issues. We then synthesize 12 recurring relationship families between training-data issues and generated-code outcomes, tracing each to its supporting papers, evidence basis, and limitations. We also synthesize detection and mitigation techniques across the data, model, and generation lifecycle. The findings position data curation as one layer of code-generation quality assurance coordinated with model- and inference-level controls, and identify provenance and controlled attribution as open research needs. Our repository is available at https://github.com/SYSUSELab/From-Data-to-Code.

Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.title: InterType: Breaking the Single-Function Barrier in Neural Binary Type Inference
Software Engineering (Dynamic Analysis &.summary: Variable type recovery is a critical task in binary reverse engineering, enabling downstream applications such as vulnerability discovery, malware analysis, and security enforcement. While recent Transformer-based models have demonstrated strong performance in type inference by learning instruction-level semantics, they predominantly operate within single-function boundaries (i.e. intra-procedural analysis), ignoring the rich type constraints that propagate across function calls. Empirical studies have shown that nearly 44% of variables in real-world binaries propagate across function boundaries as arguments or return values, representing a significant source of type information that intra-procedural models cannot exploit. In this paper, we propose InterType, a method that embeds inter-procedural analysis into a pre-trained Transformer model for binary type recovery. Our approach builds on CodeArt, a state-of-the-art Transformer model for stripped binary analysis, and extends it by incorporating caller-callee data flow dependencies during fine-tuning. Specifically, we extract data flow dependence for each caller-callee pair from disassembled binaries and construct training instances that provide the model with cross-function context. By exposing the Transformer to inter-procedural variable propagation patterns, our model learns to resolve types that depend on cross-function data flow. We evaluate InterType on the coreutils benchmark compiled with optimization levels O0 through O3. On O1 binaries, InterType improves recall by 2.76 percentage points, from 89.00% for the intra-procedural CodeArt baseline to 91.76%, corresponding to a 25.1% reduction in recall error rate (1 - recall).

Security & Program Analysis.title: Janus: a Playground for User-Involved Agentic Permission Management
Security & Program Analysis.summary: AI agents that autonomously execute tool calls on a user's behalf raise pressing questions about permission management: what role could users play, and what role should they play? Despite many proposed approaches, the user's role in agentic permission management remains underexplored. We introduce Janus, a playground system for implementing and evaluating user-involved agentic permission management designs. Janus consists of two components: Janus-Core, a modular agentic system supporting a diverse spectrum of permission management designs, and Janus-Harness, an automated evaluation framework. Grounded in a conceptual model that identifies key design axes for user involvement, we implement six permission assistants spanning the design space and evaluate them across three scenarios with four subscenarios each and three synthetic responders. We demonstrate that user involvement is critical and can strengthen privacy and security and that user behavior such as permission fatigue must be accounted for in system design. No single design performs optimally across all contexts, motivating a more principled and context-sensitive approach to deploying permission assistants in agentic systems. Janus is publicly available to support future investigation into this dimension of agentic system design.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: To appear in 48th IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (2027)

Security & Program Analysis.title: CyberCane: a privacy-bounded neuro-symbolic retrieval framework for phishing detection under distribution shift
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Organizations usually calibrate phishing detectors on public corpora, because privacy rules make their own labeled legitimate mail hard to collect. This practice breaks the false-positive budget of trained detectors: calibrated for a 1% false-positive rate (FPR) on older public mail and deployed on DataPhish 2025, they realize 20.2-22.9% FPR, 9-94 times the budget across three calibration sources. The cause is calibration transfer, not ranking: the classifiers separate the deployment mail well, but their thresholds do not transfer. We introduce CyberCane, a privacy-bounded neuro-symbolic detector that scores email only by similarity to known phishing in a redacted, training-only index, plus deterministic rules, and calibrates verdicts to an explicit FPR budget. Because legitimate mail never enters its score, only its threshold depends on the calibration source. Under the same shift CyberCane realizes 5.4% FPR at 86.4% recall, reducing the overrun 2.7-6.1 times across sources, seeds, a second shift family, and a local embedder. A segment-level variant, scoring an email's most phishing-like part, lowers the realized FPR a further 1.2-2.7 times at equal ranking quality and withstands benign padding. CyberCane screens an email locally in 0.20 s, sending no text out; a 70B zero-shot LLM ranks better at strict FPR but is 14-24 times slower and must receive each email. We also show that LLM rewriting does not evade embedding-based detectors and that a random split of DataPhish 2025 leaks 96% of its test set. All protocols were fixed in advance, and the released splits and code let a deployer measure realized FPR before trusting a budget.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Code: https://github.com/sbhakim/Cybercane

Security & Program Analysis.title: Same Data, Different Bytes: Serialization-Invariant Integrity Checks for Agent-Published Datasets
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Agent networks require reliable ways for requesting agents to verify where data is located, how it can be accessed, and whether the data received matches what the data owner made available. Checksum mismatches can reflect either altered content or serialization differences that preserve data equivalence under specified rules. Data identification mechanisms for agents, such as DataFacts, describe where data can be accessed and provide checksums for checking received data against published references. We propose a serialization-invariant identification method that assigns the same identifier to data representations equivalent under explicit rules. We use DataFacts as a case study, retaining its existing checksum alongside the proposed identifier. In a controlled agent study, we compare the proposed configuration with ordinary-tool and checksum baselines across equivalent re-encodings, altered content, and unavailable references. The study includes three model tiers from each of two providers. For equivalent re-encodings, the proposed configuration increased expected-outcome rates by 80.4 percentage points over the ordinary-tool baseline and by 70.2 percentage points over the checksum baseline. The proposed configuration also increased evidence-supported rejection of altered content by 3.5 percentage points over the checksum baseline. We contribute a serialization-invariant identification method with explicit equivalence rules, an integration approach illustrated through DataFacts, and an empirical evaluation against ordinary-tool and checksum baselines.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 4 pages. Accepted at the NANDA Workshop, IEEE TPS-ISA 2026

Security & Program Analysis.title: CAT-RAG: Improving Secure Code Generation with Category-Aware Agentic Retrieval
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Despite rapid progress in LLM-based code generation, security vulnerabilities remain widespread, and retrieval-augmented code generation (RACG) can further amplify risk when retrieved knowledge is verbose or vulnerable to poisoning. Existing secure RACG approaches inject security knowledge at a fine-grained vulnerability level, causing prompt overhead and diluted model attention when a query implicates multiple related weaknesses. We propose CAT-RAG, an agentic security category-aware retrieval-augmented code generation framework. CAT-RAG performs adaptive category selection via an LLM as a categorizer agent and operates either as a standalone security layer or as a drop-in add-on to RACG pipelines, requiring no modification to the underlying model. We replace CWE-level retrieval with compact, language-specific security categories. These categories provide a higher-level abstraction over individual CWE weaknesses, organizing them by the security concern they share, such as Input Validation and Injection Attacks, rather than merely grouping related entries. Each category consolidates best practices and secure code examples into a single, prompt-efficient representation. We perform a comprehensive evaluation across CyberSecEval, CodeGuard+, and HumanEval. On CyberSecEval, CAT-RAG nearly doubles the secure code generation improvement over the state of the art (23.57% vs. 12.11%) while reducing token overhead by 41.71%.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Peer Pressure: Execution-Verified Co-Evolution of Attacker and Defender Populations for Code Security
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
LLM code agents increasingly ship code with little oversight, yet defenders trained on static vulnerability datasets fall behind adapting adversaries. We co-train attacker and defender instead, and let execution decide every reward: an attacker (Red) edits a real repository and earns nothing unless its patch applies, builds, passes the tests, completes its development task and reproduces a real exploit in an isolated container, whose path also labels the entry point, the critical operation and the trace between them.
  Peer-Relative Policy Optimization (PRPO) makes both sides populations of LoRA adapters over one frozen base and credits each against same-role peers that faced an identical condition, placing the population inside the policy-gradient baseline rather than the opponent pool, with a tournament preserving diversity. Matching cancels the condition's difficulty: at equal coverage it is worth 2.3 points of balanced accuracy over a baseline computed on other conditions, and it matches a within-policy control at half the verifier spend.
  PRPO's 7B diff reviewer reaches 64.8% balanced accuracy on four unseen applications in three untrained languages, 5.5 points above supervised security fine-tuning and 4.4 above a frozen frontier reviewer (Claude Opus 4.8), which it leads by 15.8 on the application it trains on. Its 9B repository agent recovers 23 of 172 held-out VulnGym advisories, against 10 after supervised fine-tuning and 7 for the same backbone untrained under the same scaffold, and locates 17 of 43 reachable entry points against 13 for mini-swe-agent with GLM-5.2. Run unchanged on jailbreak defense, the same algorithm matches or exceeds WildGuard's static F1 at equal corpus and model size. Under a judge distinct from its training oracle it cuts attack success from 36.0% to 4.6%, against WildGuard's 8.9%.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Preprint. Under Review

Security & Program Analysis.title: The One-Pixel of Reasoning: One Truthful Relation Is Enough to Mislead LLM Agents
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Can one sentence manipulate an agent's belief by targeting a single implicit warrant linking evidence to a conclusion? In this paper, we introduce the one-relation attack (ORA), a novel cognitive attack on this inferential relation. ORA localizes a critical implicit warrant and performs a one-relation intervention using a single source-grounded sentence that qualifies this warrant and steers the agent toward an incorrect belief. Across eighteen models on biomedical inference and vulnerability detection, best-of-$10 attacks overturn initially correct answers at mean rates of 54.9% for proprietary and 80.0% for open-weight models. Attacks also transfer without victim feedback, and paired controls support the roles of targeting and qualification. Moreover, successful sentences can pass source-support checks and evade identification, and multi-agent debate raises team error from 50.0% to 59.5% in our balanced stress test. These findings establish implicit warrants as a cognitive attack surface for manipulating agents' beliefs.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Under Review

Security & Program Analysis.title: The Missing Compliance Class: LLM Graders That Collapse Jailbreak Success, and a Free Check
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Jailbreak papers report an attack success rate, the share of responses that deliver the harmful request, and read it as a property of the target model. We hold the target model, the prompts and the responses fixed and change only the grader. Three dense graders of 8B and 9B parameters, from three model families, move compliant responses to the neighbouring class, evasion, instead of scattering them across classes. One of them assigns the compliance label zero times in 900 responses. This class collapse also appears on new harmful requests, on a target model from a third family, and in a held-out 7B grader from a fourth family. Per-class label counts expose it at no cost and without human labels. The collapse decides how the rate behaves under a change of grader. On two corpora of 900 responses and eight graders, the compliance rate differs by a factor of 22 to 25, while the non-refusal rate differs by 18 to 23 percentage points. Without the three collapsing graders, compliance differs by a factor of 1.7 to 2.8 on all four corpora, and non-refusal still differs by 10 to 22 points. These results do not change when every grader is called once. We propose a reporting minimum that keeps the compliance rate and adds its per-class label counts and the named grader. Beside it goes the non-refusal rate, whose disagreement across graders is additive.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 29 pages, 6 figures, 17 tables. Code and labels: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/missing-compliance-class-4F6F

Security & Program Analysis.title: Quantifying Memorization and Privacy Risks in Genomic Language Models
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Genomic language models (GLMs) have emerged as powerful tools for learning representations of DNA sequences, enabling advances in variant prediction, regulatory element identification, and cross-task transfer learning. However, as these models are increasingly trained or fine-tuned on sensitive genomic cohorts, they risk memorizing specific sequences from their training data, raising serious concerns around privacy, data leakage, and regulatory compliance. Despite growing awareness of memorization risks in general-purpose language models, little systematic evaluation exists for these risks in the genomic domain, where data exhibit unique properties such as a fixed nucleotide alphabet, strong biological structure, and individual identifiability. We present a comprehensive, multi-vector privacy evaluation framework designed to quantify memorization risks in GLMs. Our approach integrates three complementary risk assessment methodologies: perplexity-based detection, canary sequence extraction, and membership inference. These are combined into a unified evaluation pipeline that produces a worst-case memorization risk score. To enable controlled evaluation, we plant canary sequences at varying repetition rates into both synthetic and real genomic datasets, allowing precise quantification of how repetition and training dynamics influence memorization. We evaluate our framework across multiple GLM architectures, examining the relationship between sequence repetition, model capacity, and memorization risk. Our results establish that GLMs exhibit measurable memorization and that the degree of memorization varies across architectures and training regimes. These findings reveal that no single attack vector captures the full scope of memorization risk, underscoring the need for multi-vector privacy auditing as a standard practice for genomic AI systems.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Accepted at ACM BCB 2026

Security & Program Analysis.title: Consistency Is the Attack Surface: Detecting Coordinated Retrieval Poisoning with Embedding Geometry
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Consistency-based defenses for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) rest on an assumption that a sparse adversary breaks: a poisoning campaign may modify a negligible fraction of the corpus, yet retrieval concentrates its passages into the reader's context. Across four Natural Questions retrieval seeds, at least one injection reaches the top-5 in 94.1% of targeted query--seed rows, and all three form a retrieved majority in 52.9%. Under our short-answer protocol, RobustRAG and ReliabilityRAG reach exposure-conditional attack success 0.512, against 0.576 for undefended RAG, while lowering clean accuracy from 0.328 to 0.216. Coordination, however, leaves a fingerprint: a dense, query-anchored component in the evidence embedding geometry. CoordGuard audits this structure from robustly normalized query-weighted affinities, without poison labels, correct answers, or reader gradients. Its always-filter mode suppresses the selected component whenever one forms; a benign-calibrated gate suppresses it only at unusually high scores and traces a robustness--utility frontier. Pooling four retrieval seeds, e5 always-filtering reduces $\mathrm{ASR}_{\mathrm{exp}}$ to 0.167 overall and 0.138 on parametrically unknown queries, at a 13.6-point clean cost, while a Contriever gate retains clean accuracy 0.315 at $\mathrm{ASR}_{\mathrm{exp}}=0.331$. The reduction transfers across two readers, three tasks, and multiple retriever--auditor pairs, and count-matched controls attribute it to component-targeted removal rather than deletion volume. These findings recast poison detection from judging truth to auditing the structure of retrieved evidence.

Security & Program Analysis.title: The Feasibility of Topic-Based Watermarking on Academic Peer Reviews
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into academic workflows, with many conferences and journals permitting their use for tasks such as language refinement and literature summarization. However, their use in peer review remains prohibited due to concerns around confidentiality breaches, hallucinated content, and inconsistent evaluations. As LLM-generated text becomes more indistinguishable from human writing, there is a growing need for reliable attribution mechanisms to preserve the integrity of the review process. In this work, we evaluate topic-based watermarking (TBW), a semantic-aware technique designed to embed detectable signals into LLM-generated text. We conduct a systematic assessment across multiple LLM configurations, including base, few-shot, and fine-tuned variants, using authentic peer review data from academic conferences. Our results show that TBW maintains review quality relative to non-watermarked outputs, while demonstrating robust detection performance under paraphrasing. These findings highlight the viability of TBW as a minimally intrusive and practical solution for LLM attribution in peer review settings.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Accepted at IJCNLP-AACL 25 Findings

Security & Program Analysis.title: Authenticated Contradictions from Desynchronized Provenance and Watermarking
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Cryptographic provenance standards such as C2PA and invisible watermarking are positioned as complementary defenses for content authentication, yet the two verification layers are technically independent: neither conditions on the output of the other. This work formalizes and empirically demonstrates the $\textit{Integrity Clash}$, a condition in which a digital asset carries a cryptographically valid C2PA manifest asserting human authorship while its pixels simultaneously carry a watermark identifying it as AI-generated, with both signals passing their respective verification checks in isolation. We construct metadata washing workflows that produce these authenticated fakes through standard editing pipelines, requiring no cryptographic compromise, only the semantic omission of a single assertion field permitted by the current C2PA specification. To close this gap, we propose a cross-layer audit protocol that jointly evaluates provenance metadata and watermark detection status, achieving 100% classification accuracy across 3,500 test images spanning four conflict-matrix states and three realistic perturbation conditions. Our results demonstrate that the gap between these verification layers is unnecessary and technically straightforward to close.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Accepted at CVPR 2026 Workshop Authenticity & Provenance in the Age of AI (APAI)

Security & Program Analysis.title: Topic-Based Watermarks for Large Language Models
Security & Program Analysis.summary: The indistinguishability of large language model (LLM) output from human-authored content poses significant challenges, raising concerns about potential misuse of AI-generated text and its influence on future model training. Watermarking algorithms offer a viable solution by embedding detectable signatures into generated text. However, existing watermarking methods often involve trade-offs among attack robustness, generation quality, and additional overhead such as specialized frameworks or complex integrations. We propose a lightweight, topic-guided watermarking scheme for LLMs that partitions the vocabulary into topic-aligned token subsets. Given an input prompt, the scheme selects a relevant topic-specific token list, effectively "green-listing" semantically aligned tokens to embed robust marks while preserving fluency and coherence. Experimental results across multiple LLMs and state-of-the-art benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves text quality comparable to industry-leading systems and simultaneously improves watermark robustness against paraphrasing and lexical perturbation attacks, with minimal performance overhead. Our approach avoids reliance on additional mechanisms beyond standard text generation pipelines, enabling straightforward adoption and suggesting a practical path toward globally consistent watermarking of AI-generated content.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Accepted at ACL 2026 Findings

Security & Program Analysis.title: From Trust Scores to Driver Decisions: An Abstaining Evidential Decision Layer for Event Validation in VANETs
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Trust management in vehicular ad hoc networks is highly active, yet the decision that a driver needs, whether a reported event is real, has received far less attention; the schemes that make it force every decision into two outcomes, even on thin or conflicting evidence. This paper presents CREST, a vehicle-side event-decision framework that can withhold a decision its evidence does not support. Each vehicle weights the reports it holds by the trust, proximity and freshness of their senders, fuses them with Yager's rule, and decides only when the fused margin reaches an abstention threshold. Abstention is a waiting state: a vehicle still unsure at the event is resolved by an explicit application policy, which makes the trade-off between missed hazards and unnecessary detours visible. CREST requires only a scalar trust per reporter and is built here on an evidential trust model whose consensus and revocation steps are updated to support the decision layer. A single report is shown to change the decision margin by at most its weight, which bounds the influence of an attacker coalition by its trust. In a pre-registered simulation study with fourteen attacks, including position spoofing and trust-gated camouflage, and with all unspecified parameters of all systems tuned by the same procedure, CREST reduces the decision error of two published trust-based dissemination systems from 0.162 and 0.106 to 0.051. With the best-guess policy it also lowers both missed and unnecessary reroutes and outperforms the forced binary rule on both error types in every cell.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Instruction Self-Arbitration Is Not a Trust Boundary: Configuration-Dependent Tool Calls and External Enforcement in LLM Agents
Security & Program Analysis.summary: LLM agents receive instructions from system prompts, users, memory and tools, and labels inside a shared context are not an enforceable trust boundary. We study how measurement and configuration choices change what benign file-deletion tasks on gateway-labelled endpoints appear to show (an availability-selected roster) and test an external reference monitor. The original keyword flag for detecting fabricated authority mostly matched negated phrases: two blind judges flagged the claim as fabricated in at most 1 of 150 GPT-4.1-mini responses. In a fully logged reflection re-run, responses that both express doubt and delete are rare after a reflection instruction (25 of 509 executions), and a casual request that gives a reason but claims no authority is executed by all ten endpoints. Source-format cues are linearly decodable (97.5-100% probe accuracy, four open-weight models), but a pre-specified crossed-probe test halted and gives no interpretable evidence of an abstract provenance representation, and steering did not move tool mention (0 of 1,895 trials, mention-scored). On the same 14,294 diverse-prompt trials across 29 endpoints, the rule fixed before collection gives an endpoint mean of 1.21%; a path-based reading chosen after the data were seen gives 12.9% [6.6-20.1%, 29 models]; any delete call gives 20.2%. In 1,350 sandbox trials, all 750 forged, tampered, replayed and unsigned records were rejected at admission and no file outside a token's scope was removed (a functional-correctness test, not a robustness estimate). Semantic authorisation remains open: a deputy with a valid scoped token induced in-scope deletions in 31/42 trials, and legitimate privileged requests produced at least one in-scope deletion in 120/150 (144/150 and 36/42 with a larger output limit).
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 68 pages, 4 figures. Paper only. v2 shortens the paper, retitles it, corrects the diverse-prompt scoring (12.9% for delete calls on the protected path or a parent; 1.21% under the v1 rule), narrows "recognition" to decodable surface cues plus elicited doubt, and adds reflection controls and a sandbox test of external enforcement. The Version Note lists all changes

Security & Program Analysis.title: LLM Trojans that Increase Response Lengths and Cost
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Management of the token-based costs of using LLMs has emerged as a significant problem. Some frontier-model providers charge five times per response token than per prompt token, while others offer prefilling discounts for prompt tokens. In this paper, we devise a defense against a new data-poisoning attack that plants a Trojan which increases the length of the response (and hence the cost to the user) when its trigger is present in the prompt. In particular, we demonstrate how a subtle Trojan may trigger on semantically similar instructions of an instruction fine-tuned LLM.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Heart Signal (ECG) as Vibration Signature for Human Authentication Using TinyML
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Ensuring data security in the era of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and deepfake technology requires robust biometric systems. Conventional methods such as facial recognition, iris scans, fingerprints, and voice recognition are increasingly vulnerable to spoofing and provide only one-time authentication at login. This study introduces an Electrocardiogram (ECG) based authentication framework, compared with Photoplethysmography (PPG), leveraging Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) for deployment on resource-constrained microcontroller units (MCUs). The proposed method enables continuous authentication, offering ongoing verification throughout device usage, which conventional biometrics cannot achieve. It also serves as a password-free solution, reducing risks of credential loss, theft, or reuse. However, ECG signals vary with physical activity, health conditions, age, and emotional states, requiring robust signal processing and learning algorithms. To address this, efficient TinyML models were designed to mitigate recognition errors from noisy real-time data. Experiments used single-lead ECG signals (Lead I) from UofTDB, MIT-BIH Arrhythmia, MIT-BIH Noise Stress Test, and PTB databases. Spectrograms and spectral features were extracted to train Deep Neural Network (DNN), 1D CNN, and 2D CNN models within the Edge Impulse platform, achieving 98% accuracy. The trained model was converted into TinyML format and deployed on an Espressif ESP-EYE (ESP32, 240 MHz). Support Vector Machine (SVM) models were also applied for benchmarking. By analyzing the number of heartbeats required for reliable recognition, the results show that averaging multiple signals improves tolerance to noise and enhances accuracy. Overall, ECG-based authentication demonstrates strong potential as a secure, real-time, and continuously verifiable method for personal identification on wearable and edge devices.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Collaborative Hand Drawing to Conceptualize Usable Privacy and Security Research Problems: Students' Perspectives (Extended Version)
Security & Program Analysis.summary: In this paper, we explore students' perspectives on incorporating hand drawing to conceptualize usable privacy and security research problems. We surveyed 64 female students who participated in an in-class collaborative hand drawing activity to conceptualize usable privacy and security research problems as part of a group-based student research project on usable privacy and security in an information and computer security course for undergraduate students. Our survey responses suggest that students perceived the drawing exercise positively. That is, they found it helpful in several aspects, enjoyable, and they recommend it to other students taking the course. The students also said that they would like to have such an exercise in other courses, such as Principles of Human-Computer Interaction and Fundamentals of Data Networks. Only three students mentioned downsides of the exercise, namely doubts about their drawing skills. Our results provide useful insights for educators seeking to enhance the student learning experience.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: This document is the authors' extended preprint for a short paper in the proceedings of Koli Calling'26, ACM (DOI: 10.1145/3856208.3856277)

Security & Program Analysis.title: SecODD: Adapting the Operational Design Domain from Driving Autonomy to Autonomous Cyber Defense
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Security operations centers are beginning to delegate detection, triage, and containment to Autonomous Cyber Defense (ACD) agents at execution time. Erroneous high-impact playbooks can disrupt critical services and create accountability gaps among deployers, SOC supervisors, vendors, managed service providers, and infrastructure providers. We propose SecODD, an execution-time governance framework for ACD that adapts the Operational Design Domain concept from autonomous-vehicle regulation to cyber autonomy. It defines the authorized scope of automated defensive actions, models when meaningful human intervention must remain possible, and specifies auditable due-care conditions through a Mitigation Safe Harbor. Four engineering requirements---tamper-evident logging, human-in-the-loop orchestration, rollback playbooks, and safe-state transition controls---are evaluated through a per-scenario audit matrix that illustrates how two ACD failure modes can be translated into pass/fail audit outcomes. The result is an evidence-oriented framework that authorizes ACD only when autonomous actions are bounded, interruptible, recoverable, and reconstructable from evidence.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 13 pages, 5 tables

Security & Program Analysis.title: Cheap to Hypothesize, Costly to Verify: The Defense Surface of Agentic Vulnerability Discovery
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Autonomous LLM agents turn vulnerability discovery into a repository-scale search: they generate many vulnerability hypotheses but can verify only a subset under a finite budget. We show that autonomous vulnerability discovery exhibits a hypothesis-verification asymmetry, where verifying a candidate hypothesis through reachability analysis, execution, and proof-of-concept construction is substantially more expensive than forming it. Under a finite resource budget, this makes autonomous discovery a resource-bounded selective-verification process, further exposing verification effort as a unique defense surface. We present RedHerring, which inserts certifiably safe decoys that divert verification effort from real vulnerabilities. Each decoy combines a CVE-derived vulnerability chain that attracts verification with a false bridge that keeps its dangerous sink unreachable. A private certificate lets the defender verify this property efficiently, while establishing the same fact from the released repository requires solving a computationally hard problem. RedHerring further adapts each decoy to the target repository so that it reads as ordinary program logic. Across 33 OSS-Fuzz projects, 70 evaluation instances, and five models under matched budgets, RedHerring reduces real vulnerabilities discovered by 38.7-60.4%. Trajectory analysis shows that agents spend 30.6-51.5% of completion tokens and an estimated 32.5-49.9% of runtime verifying decoys, showing that RedHerring redirects a substantial fraction of the fixed search budget toward decoys. When explicitly informed that decoys may be present, the agent adapts its search strategy, yet RedHerring still reduces vulnerabilities discovered by 37.2% relative to an informed Baseline, showing that its effectiveness does not depend on decoy secrecy.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Project page: https://xxbai.space/redherring/

Security & Program Analysis.title: Fast \(\ell_\infty\)-Reduction of Rank-2 Lattices in $\mathbb{R}^n$ via a New Reduced-Basis Notion
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
The shortest vector problem (SVP) under the infinity norm ($\ell_\infty$-norm) is an important lattice problem with applications in lattice-based cryptography. In particular, the security analysis of the post-quantum signature standard ML-DSA highlights the importance of finding short solutions satisfying infinity-norm constraints, rather than only Euclidean norm bounds. However, most existing lattice reduction algorithms are developed for the Euclidean norm, while dedicated studies under the infinity norm remain limited.
  In this work, we focus on rank-two lattices in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and introduce a new notion of reduced basis under the infinity norm. Based on this definition, we propose an efficient lattice basis reduction algorithm that performs a multi-dimensional analogue of Euclidean division using a dominant coordinate of the basis vectors. Each non-terminal iteration guarantees a factor-two decrease of the maximum infinity norm of the basis vectors. We prove that the algorithm terminates and achieves a bit complexity of $O(nT^2)$, matching the asymptotic complexity order of the classical Lagrange--Gauss reduction. Moreover, the proposed algorithm saves at least $2n$ multiplications per iteration compared with the classical approach. Experiments demonstrate significant runtime improvements, especially for high-dimensional lattices. This work provides a foundation for developing lattice reduction techniques under the infinity norm.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 21 pages, 0figures

Security & Program Analysis.title: A Quantum Approach For Reducing Communications in Classical Secure Computations with Long Outputs
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
How could quantum cryptography help us achieve what are not achievable in classical cryptography? In this work we study the classical cryptographic problem that two parties would like to perform secure computations with long outputs. As a basic primitive and example, we first consider the following problem which we call secure function sampling with long outputs: suppose $f:\{0,1\}^n\rightarrow \{0,1\}^m$ is a public, efficient classical function, where $m$ is big; Alice would like to sample $x$ from its domain and sends $f(x)$ to Bob; what Bob knows should be no more than $f(x)$ even if it behaves maliciously. Classical cryptography, like FHE and succinct arguments [Gen09,Kil92,HW15], allows us to achieve this task within communication complexity $O(n+m)$; could we achieve this task with communication complexity independent of $m$?
  In this work, we first design a quantum cryptographic protocol that achieves secure function sampling with approximate security, within $O(n)$ communication (omitting the dependency on the security parameter and error tolerance). We also prove the classical impossibility using techniques in [HW15], which means that our protocol indeed achieves a type of quantum advantage. Building on the secure function sampling protocol, we further construct protocols for general secure two-party computations [Yao86,GB01] with approximate security, with communication complexity only depending on the input length and the targeted security. In terms of the assumptions, we construct protocols for these problems assuming only the existence of collapsing hash functions [Unr16]; what's more, we also construct a classical-channel protocol for these problems additionally assuming the existence of noisy trapdoor claw-free functions [BCMVV,BKVV].

Security & Program Analysis.title: Narratives Mislead: An Empirical Study of How LLMs Misjudge CVSS Severity in Bug Bounty Reports
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Bug bounty platforms receive vulnerability reports faster than vendors can triage them, and Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly considered for assigning the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) severity that drives prioritization. Prior evaluations score short CVE descriptions and report accuracy, but deployment depends on how models err, not only how often. CVSS gives each metric a formal meaning that departs from how researchers describe impact in narrative reports, and model rationales suggest that errors concentrate where the two diverge; we ask whether this pattern is systematic. From 4,281 publicly disclosed reports mined from Huntr and HackerOne, we build a benchmark of 240 Huntr reports with vendor-validated CVSS vectors and evaluate eight LLMs under four prompting strategies and fine-tuning, measuring errors by severity class and score and analysing sub-vectors on individual reports. The best prompting configuration reaches only 49.58% level accuracy, ten points above always predicting the majority level, and fine-tuning a 7B model raises this to at most 56.25%, an optimistic upper bound. Errors are directional: models overestimate far more often than they underestimate, and they almost never recognize low-severity vulnerabilities. We trace these errors to three semantic boundaries that the specification draws and narrative reports blur: potential versus realized impact, impact magnitude versus authorization scope, and uncertainty versus the worst case. Because the violations originate partly in the report, we close with an exploratory case study: on four reports, a boundary-aligned, exploit-free report structure lowered a frontier model's score where the narrative invited an unclaimed account takeover, but left the metrics a report does not settle open, and the two published labels disagreed on three of the four reports.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 10 pages,6 figures

Security & Program Analysis.title: Mitigating Data Reconstruction Attacks in Federated Learning: Conditions, Bounds, and Theoretical Guarantees
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Privacy attacks, particularly data reconstruction attacks, pose significant challenges to federated learning despite its promise in privacy-preserving collaborative training. This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical analysis of privacy leakage in federated learning through dual perspectives: linear algebra and optimization theory. By analyzing the client-update Jacobian, we identify conditions under which distinct data batches produce the same model update and derive a sufficient batch-size criterion for non-unique reconstruction. Through optimization theory, we establish a novel upper bound for privacy leakage that incorporates batch size, distortion extent, and other critical parameters. These theoretical insights elucidate the fundamental relationships between system parameters and privacy vulnerability, laying the groundwork for developing more robust privacy-preserving federated learning frameworks.

Security & Program Analysis.title: When Code Becomes an LLM Call: An Empirical Study of Call-Site Contracts in Agentic Systems
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Software quality has long rested on specifications that state what code must do, and on testing and verification that check that the code does it. Agentic systems change this foundation: they replace parts of their logic, such as choosing the next tool, judging whether an action is allowed, or writing code to run, with calls to a large language model (LLM). The program still relies on what this logic must guarantee, but the model's behavior is not fixed by code, varies across runs, and can be steered by its input. The guarantee must therefore come from the program around each LLM call site, as a contract of pre-conditions, prompt constraints, and post-conditions. We present an empirical study of these contracts in 496 LLM call sites of 40 popular open-source agentic systems (13.4 MLOC, four languages). Using a multi-agent pipeline validated by 17,428 human judgments, we trace where every model output flows, derive an expected contract for each call site without access to its code, and compare it with the contract that the code implements. We find that 48% of LLM outputs reach control flow or execution, and 73% of these never reach a person. Programs enforce 78% of their constraints in code, but in the prompt, 67% of the constraints are only requested from the model. Although 82% of call sites are checked before and after the call, 63% of the expected constraints are unmet and only 5.3% of call sites satisfy their whole contract; ten recurring patterns explain 99% of the gaps. 38 mechanisms behind these gaps trigger at runtime, and a small code fix that enforces the expected constraint stops all 38. Our results show that the presence of checks says little about their adequacy, and we derive implications for agent developers, framework maintainers, and researchers.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 18 pages

Security & Program Analysis.title: Combining LLM and Dynamic Analysis for Universal Testing of Static Application Security Testing Tools
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Static application security testing (SAST) tools help detect potential software vulnerabilities, but they themselves contain faults undermining reliability and usability. Automated testing can address these issues, yet current techniques suffer from limited program transformation diversity and lack mechanisms to verify generated variants, leading to reduced fault detection and high manual effort. We present LLM4SAST, the first universal framework detecting faults in SAST tools using large language models and dynamic feedback. Our key insight is leveraging LLMs to understand and transform code in diverse programming languages. We design novel metamorphic relations with transformations to guide variant generation, using an LLM to produce multi-language variants that satisfy these relations. To reduce erroneous variants and identify unique faults, we propose two heuristics: dynamic-feedback-driven selection and program-differencing-based clustering. For each metamorphic relation, a report-centric test oracle detects variants that fail tests and identifies underlying faults by differentially analyzing SAST reports of the seed program and its variants. LLM4SAST identified 66 unique faults across six SAST tools, with 32 confirmed or fixed after being reported to developers, demonstrating effectiveness. The proposed heuristics eliminate 47.8% of false positives, and LLM4SAST detects 3.4 times more faults while requiring only 39.8% of the variants compared to existing approaches.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Evaluating and Improving Static Application Security Testing Tools for Rust
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Rust has become a popular systems programming language in recent years because of its strong guarantees on memory and concurrency safety. Many types of system software have been re-implemented in Rust. However, Rust programs can still suffer from common memory and concurrency vulnerabilities due to unsafe code and misunderstandings of its complex mechanisms. To mitigate such vulnerabilities, developers often rely on static application security testing (SAST) tools. However, the effectiveness of existing Rust SAST tools on real-world vulnerabilities remains underexplored. In this paper, we first conduct an empirical evaluation of mainstream Rust SAST tools using security vulnerabilities identified in real-world Rust applications. We systematically assess their effectiveness, uncover common weaknesses, and analyze the root causes behind them. Motivated by the study, we propose TRUST, a large language model (LLM)-assisted automated testing framework. TRUST automatically analyzes the official Rust reference to derive and implement semantics-preserving transformations. It leverages these transformations to generate mutant programs for evaluating Rust SAST tools and uncovering potential faults within them. Overall, TRUST has revealed 46 faults across six popular SAST tools, 17 of which have been confirmed. In addition, our study yields ten empirical findings and four practical lessons that provide actionable guidance for developing more effective, robust, and maintainable Rust SAST tools.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Effective Construction of Feature Database of Fingerprinting Functions for Code-Clone SCA
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
In contemporary software development, the extensive adoption of third-party libraries has become standard practice to avoid reinventing the wheel. This trend is particularly evident in programming ecosystems that lack mature package managers, such as C/C++. Within this context, Code Clone Detection (CCD) techniques have emerged as essential tools for identifying instances of code reuse, thereby mitigating security and legal concerns. Despite significant advances in CCD algorithms, a notable gap persists between academic tools and real-world applications. This disparity primarily arises because academic tools rely on experimental datasets composed of a limited number of indexed repositories, whereas real-world applications require a much broader scope of code sources.
  To address this challenge, we propose a novel, systematic approach for selecting appropriate open-source repositories to construct a more effective CCD feature dataset. Our method, OSSScope, employs a greedy algorithm to analyze the diversity of fingerprinting functions across 2.55 million C repositories on GitHub, maximizing unique fingerprinting functions while minimizing the number of repositories required. OSSScope compiles an optimal feature dataset containing 61 million fingerprinting functions from 190K repositories, resulting in a 22.65% improvement in recall over SOTA tools, and covers over 95% of the features from other sources. Leveraging the selected repositories, we introduce RClassifier, a lightweight classification model that determines whether a repository should be included, streamlining construction for migration to other language ecosystems. Our evaluation of RClassifier in the Golang ecosystem validates its effectiveness, achieving recall comparable to the dataset produced by OSSScope.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Private Evaluation of High-Dimensional Functions
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
We study differentially private black-box evaluation of arbitrary high-dimensional functions. Given a dataset $S$ and query access to a function $f$---whose sensitivity may be unknown or unbounded---the goal is to privately output an approximation to $f(S)$. The black-box evaluator can only query the value of $f$ over a down neighborhood of $S$ (i.e., those subsets of $S$ that are obtained by removing a bounded number of elements from $S$). We design generic black-box evaluators for both pure and approximate differential privacy through a reduction to high-dimensional private quasi-concave optimization (QCO).
  Our black-box evaluator enjoys a geometric notion of utility. Consider the vectors obtained by applying $f$ on sets in a down neighborhood of $S$. With high probability, the evaluator's output is guaranteed to be in the convex hull of these vectors.
  Our work generalizes the result of Linder et al. [LRSS25] for real-valued function evaluation to high dimensions. It also recovers the private center-point guarantees of Beimel et al. [BMNS19], with an explicit additive approximation to maximum Tukey depth. We also apply our evaluators to user-level quasi-concave and convex optimization, showing how they can improve upon the sample-and-aggregate baseline of Nissim et al. [NRS07] by replacing the multiplicative data overhead with an additive overhead.
  Finally, we show that our formulation of high dimensional black-box evaluation and high dimensional private QCO are equivalent up to a factor of the dimension: the hardest private evaluation instances already arise from the cases that $f$ is a (non-private) quasi-concave optimizer.

Security & Program Analysis.title: Memory-Induced Tool-Drift in LLM Agents
Security & Program Analysis.summary: LLM agents increasingly combine long-term memory for personalization with tool calling for taking actions. We study a failure of this combination: personality-driven preferences stored in memory (e.g., cost-consciousness, impatience, risk tolerance) silently shifting tool-call parameters in contexts where they do not apply. We call this memory-induced tool-drift and stress-test it with MEMDRIFT, an iteratively refined benchmark of 105 scenarios spanning five bias dimensions and seven professional domains. Measured as excess parameter degradation over a neutral-memory baseline, biased memories in MEMDRIFT induce drift in all eight models we evaluate, raising degradation rates to 0.38--0.83 versus 0.05--0.12 for neutral memories. The drift persists under three widely used memory frameworks. A vulnerability audit of 6,062 tools across 288 MCP servers demonstrates that real-world tools are also susceptible to this failure mode. Mechanistically, we find that biased memories act as implicit steering vectors along the same direction as explicit behavioral instructions and draw attention away from task-relevant context. Neither prompt-based defenses nor relevance filters offer a complete solution, motivating defenses at the intersection of memory management and tool calling.

Security & Program Analysis.title: A Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning Method for Heterogeneous Clients
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Federated Learning (FL) with Differential Privacy (DP) can ensure the protection of healthcare data privacy against malicious user attacks. However, FL with the DP method faces an inherent trade-off: stronger privacy protection degrades predictive accuracy due to injected noise. On the other hand, Homomorphic Encryption (HE) enables computations on encrypted data and the aggregation of encrypted gradients without introducing DP-induced noise, thereby potentially increasing the predictive accuracy. However, it may increase the computation cost. To improve the predictive accuracy while considering the computational ability of heterogeneous clients, we propose a Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning (PPML)-Hybrid method. In the proposed PPML-Hybrid method, clients distributedly select either HE or DP based on their computational resources, so that HE clients contribute noise-free updates while DP clients reduce computational overhead. Meanwhile, clients with high computational resources can flexibly adopt HE or DP according to their privacy needs. Performance evaluation on omics datasets shows that our proposed method achieves comparable predictive accuracy while significantly reducing computation time relative to HE-only. Additionally, it outperforms DP-only methods under equivalent or stricter privacy budgets.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: 6 pages, 4 figures

Security & Program Analysis.title: Defending Against Dormant Poisoning Attacks Across Language and Multimodal Agents
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Recent work shows that attackers can implant dormant malicious behaviors that remain hidden at release but emerge after benign fine-tuning. As foundation models are used as agents, whether dormant poisoning extends to harmful agent actions and multimodal settings remains unclear. We show two agentic risks: (1) harmful behaviors activated by benign fine-tuning can extend to unseen actions; (2) multiple harmful behaviors can coexist and be jointly activated by benign downstream fine-tuning. Existing defenses often rely on external safe responses, which are hard to obtain for agent actions, or a trusted clean reference model. We exploit a key property of dormant poisoning: the attacker must preserve safe behavior at release to conceal poisoning, and this behavior can serve as a safety reference. Leveraging this property, we automatically construct a Safety Buffer pairing harmful inputs with the released model's responses and benign versions generated by the same model to remove harmful intent. The Safety Buffer can replace external safe responses in existing defenses, but these defenses do not distinguish updates that weaken safety from those that preserve it, often increasing over-refusal or reducing utility. To address this limitation, we introduce LookAhead Defense, which previews benign fine-tuning updates using the Safety Buffer and penalizes only updates predicted to weaken safe behavior on harmful inputs or increase the likelihood of refusals on benign versions in the Safety Buffer. Across language models, language agents, and multimodal agents, LookAhead Defense reduces harmful behavior in agents from up to 93.9% to at most 14.2% and harmful responses in language models from up to 92.5% to at most 2.0% versus vanilla fine-tuning, while maintaining competitive utility and low over-refusal. It remains effective against other poisoning methods.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Project page: https://wonjuun.github.io/LookAhead/

Security & Program Analysis.title: Multimodal Resource-Exhaustion Attacks on Vision-Language Models via Joint Pixel-Prompt Optimization
Security & Program Analysis.summary:
Resource-exhaustion attacks against autoregressive vision-language models (VLMs) typically assume unimodal threat models, treating the image branch as the primary optimization surface while holding user-visible prompts fixed. Even recent loop-centric variants remain confined to this single-channel paradigm, leaving the exploitation of availability unexplored as a cross-modal optimization problem over jointly controllable input surfaces.
  We introduce Joint Pixel-Prompt Optimization (JPPO), the first compound adversarial framework elevating the visible prompt to a first-class adversarial variable alongside image perturbations. Under a restricted joint-input threat model, JPPO performs coupled, stagewise optimization over both the pixel and prompt surfaces. This produces synergistic cost amplification, mechanistically distinct from loop-dependent failures, exhibiting negligible loop incidence in our experiments.
  Evaluating five open-source VLM families on MS COCO and ImageNet under an 8/255 infinity-norm budget, JPPO achieves over 4.6x latency and 5.3x energy amplification on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and over 36.6x latency with 32.7x energy amplification on BLIP-2. This represents the strongest cost amplification among directly compared baselines while requiring substantially fewer optimization iterations. Ablations confirm this amplification arises from multimodal coordination rather than prompt length or isolated modalities. These findings reveal structural blind spots in current VLM serving defenses, motivating cost-aware robustness evaluation as a first-class security requirement for multimodal deployments.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Extended version of the paper accepted by ACM CCS 2026

Security & Program Analysis.title: Can Agents Keep Secrets They Were Never Told? Benchmarking Latent Privacy Risks Across Sessions with MemJoin
Security & Program Analysis.summary: To support sustained interactions and personalized assistance, agents use long-term memory to retain and combine user information across sessions. Reusing such memories can lead an agent to state a sensitive relation while completing an ordinary task that does not require it. The relation to protect and the combination of clues that reveal it may remain hidden at memory write time, when later records and tasks are still unknown. In this paper, we introduce MemJoin, a privacy benchmark of 288 synthetic analysis cases in which the complete history entails a sensitive relation, but every individual session is insufficient. We evaluate six memory systems with the same answer-generating model, alongside full-history and no-history controls. Each system writes and updates memories in session order and later retrieves context for an ordinary task, while target annotations remain with the evaluator. We separately check which target attribute values appear in stored records and retrieved context, and whether the final answer states the complete, person-linked relation. In a separate paired test on a prespecified subset, removing shared identifiers and other connecting clues can change complete-relation output while all checked target attribute values remain visible. These findings show why checking attribute visibility alone is insufficient to evaluate what records from different sessions reveal together.

Security & Program Analysis.title: COPEX: Benchmarking LLM Robustness to Adversarial Context Across Model Context Protocol (MCP) Layers
Security & Program Analysis.summary: Large language models increasingly mediate tool use in Model Context Protocol (MCP) systems, where adversarial influence may enter through user instructions, tool schemas, tool outputs, or protocol messages. Existing benchmarks often evaluate deployed agents, conflating model susceptibility with guardrails, orchestration, and general task capability. We introduce COPEX (COntext Provider EXploitation), a controlled benchmark that isolates the model as an MCP client by fixing the surrounding agent stack and varying only the tool-selecting model. COPEX covers 25 attack types instantiated as 125 scenarios across four entry surfaces: model/agent, client, server/tool, and transport. Across nine models and 3,375 trials, the mean attack success rate is 64.4%, with surface-level means ranging from 58.3% to 71.4%. Some client- and transport-level attacks succeed partly outside the model's observation or control, separating system exposure from model susceptibility. Combined input and context scanning reduces mean attack success by 49.6% on an eight-attack defense subset relative to the undefended setting. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/inspire-center/copex.
Security & Program Analysis.comment: Accepted as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Agents in the Wild

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: Anticipatory Gait Switching for Quadrupeds via Look-Ahead MDP Planning
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: Quadruped robots often switch gaits to traverse mixed terrain safely. Many practical supervisors enforce hardware constraints (e.g., dwell or guard intervals) using a transition handler. However, the switch decision itself is often driven by near-field thresholds, which can delay commitment when rough terrain is only detected shortly before contact in the local height map. We propose a lightweight height-map-only gait supervisor that unifies look-ahead and locomotion constraints in a single decision policy. A robot-centered height map is partitioned into near-, mid-, and far-field bands, each discretized into a terrain class, and band evolution is modeled as a Markov process. Gait selection is cast as a look-ahead Markov Decision Process whose transition model and cost explicitly encode platform-specific switching constraints. Indoor and outdoor experiments on a Unitree Go2 platform show reduced late switching, lower time spent using ineffective gaits on rough terrain, and improved roll stability compared to tuned reactive baselines. Overall, the MDP formulation yields anticipative constraint-aware gait switching that improves robustness without course-specific retuning.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: OccSim: Multi-kilometer Simulation with Long-horizon Occupancy World Models
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: Data-driven autonomous driving simulation has long been constrained by its heavy reliance on pre-recorded driving logs or spatial priors, such as HD maps. This fundamental dependency severely limits scalability, restricting open-ended generation capabilities to the finite scale of existing collected datasets. To break this bottleneck, we present OccSim, the first 3D occupancy world model driven simulator that requires neither HD maps nor log-derived layouts. OccSim obviates the requirement for continuous logs or HD maps; conditioned only on a single initial frame and a sequence of future ego-actions. It can stably generate over 3000 continuous frames, an 80x improvement in stable generation length over previous SoTA occupancy world models, and fuses them into maps spanning over 9 kilometers. Further qualitative stress tests show that it can roll out beyond 110K frames. OccSim is powered by two modules: W-DiT based static occupancy world model and the Layout Generator. W-DiT handles the ultra-long-horizon generation of static environments by explicitly introducing known rigid transformations in architecture design, while the Layout Generator populates the dynamic foreground with reactive agents based on the synthesized road topology. With these designs, OccSim can synthesize massive, diverse simulation streams. Extensive experiments demonstrate its downstream utility: data collected directly from OccSim can pre-train 4D semantic occupancy forecasting models to achieve up to 67% zero-shot performance on unseen data, outperforming previous asset-based simulator by 11%. When the collected data is scaled up to 5x its original size, zero-shot performance increases to 74%.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: DiPLO: Self-distilled Diffusion Planning for Loco-manipulation
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation is particularly challenging because it requires coordinating locomotion, balance, and object interaction, making it difficult to learn from limited demonstrations or from scratch through Reinforcement Learning (RL). We introduce DiPLO (self-distilled Diffusion Planning for Loco-manipulation), a framework that combines a self-distilled diffusion planner with a low-level whole-body tracking policy. Our planner is pretrained via supervised learning on motions derived from human-to-humanoid retargeting, while the tracker is trained via RL to execute them. DiPLO centers around two complementary post-training stages. First, we introduce Self-Distillation Diffusion Policy Optimisation (SD:DPO) to remove the planner's dependence on strong task conditioning, which we identify as a crucial ingredient for effective pretraining, as downstream fine-tuning does not recover comparable performance when it is omitted.. We then fine-tune this distilled model with Diffusion-Augmented Proximal Policy Optimization (DA:PPO), a maximum-entropy RL method for diffusion models, to improve task success and align generated plans with the frozen tracker's execution capabilities. Together, these stages enable motion generation through state-history and goal conditioning alone, enabling 99% task success in pick-carry-place tasks, compared to just 45% for the pretrained model. The resulting planner also generates motions for unseen object goals, with further evaluations on kicking and pushing/pulling tasks. Finally, we deploy our pipeline on the hardware, using our DA:PPO planner-tracker on a Unitree G1, achieving repeated successful executions without any real-world fine-tuning.

Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).title: Escape Without a Recipe: Maneuver-Agnostic Mars Rover Recovery from Granular Entrapment
Robotics (UAV & Autonomous Systems).summary: Wheeled planetary rovers immobilised in loose regolith have no principled recovery controller: scripted maneuvers are terrain-specific, and naive driving deepens entrapment. We introduce a recurrent policy that learns to escape without a predefined maneuver. The framework rests on a verified trap: in a continuum material point method (MPM) simulator we identify a configuration at sinkage-to-radius ratio z/r = 2.0 where the strongest of ten scripted controllers succeeds in only 7/32 trials, yet the regolith retains traction and continues to shear, confirming granular entrapment rather than a numerical artifact.
